"Frigidae" is the site of a Roman castellum located 18 km south of Lixus that is mentioned as a station on the Antonine Itinerary.
"Kastri 2" is the site of a Late Minoan settlement that is located to the west of Apodoulou, in Rethymno, Crete.
"Laodicea on the Lycus": an ancient settlement located near the modern village of Eskihisar (Eski Hissar) in Denizli Province, Turkey.

"Magliana Vecchia" is the name of the 40th urban administrative zone of the Comune di Roma. It is located to the southwest of the city center and straddles the Grande Raccordo Anulare (Ring Road) line that circles the city. The compilers of the Barrington Atlas noted that this place includes a "bridge" and a "settlement". In terms of archaeological remains, numerous sites have been identified in and around Magliana Vecchia, including a Roman bridge and several villas.

"Sioua" is the Greek reconstruction of an ancient toponym (found in Egyptian sources: S·t-wȝḥ) that encompassed some part of the western end of the Dakhla Oasis in Egypt (certainly the site now known as Deir al-Haggar was included, and possibly also Amheida).
(A)Esica, also known as Great Chesters, was a fort on the line of Hadrian's Wall.
(B)Aletium (Alezio) was a Messapic center that had ties to the Iapyges, according to Pliny. Saracens destroyed the site ca. A.D. 1000.
(H)Atria (modern Adria) was a Venetic and, later, Etruscan settlement. The city itself is likely a sixth century BC foundation.
*Argentomagus was a pre-Roman and later Roman settlement in the territory of the Bituriges tribe.
*Aurinia/Saturnia was a settlement in Etruria. Dionysius of Halicarnassus claimed it was founded by the Pelasgians. Saturnia received a Roman colony in 183 BC.
*Gariann(on)um is the site of a third-century A.D. Roman coastal fort.
*Glannoventa was a Roman fort and naval base on the coast of Cumbria.
*Letocetum was an important military post near the junction of Watling Street and Icknield Street.
*Moridunum (Carmarthen) was the civitas capital of the Demetae in Roman Wales.
*Ponte Navata, a late Roman fort on Sibrik hill, Visegrád, Hungary.
*Porsulae/Maximianopolis, also known as Mosynopolis, was a Byzantine town along the Via Egnatia in Thrace; its position is close to the modern Greek city of Komotini.
*Sedunum was the principal settlement of the Seduni.
*Tiddis (or Castellum Tidditanorum) was a Roman city located in the Constantine Province in Algeria.
A "Kenchreai in the Troad," mentioned first by Stephanus, is probably to be identified with a settlement of Roman date, located atop the Kayalı Dağ in modern Turkey.
A Berbero-Roman town of North Africa (modern Djémila in Algeria). Sometimes labeled on maps and in travel information as "Curculum".
A Black Sea colony founded by Miletus.
A Byzantine site in western Sardinia, made important by the location of a bishopric there by Torcotorio in AD 1070; now the modern city of Oristano.

A Celtic and subsequent Roman settlement at an important road junction and river crossing (modern Wels in Austria). The core of the ancient town, which evidently grew to significant size in the Roman period, is covered by the modern settlement and has only been selectively excavated.
A Celtic settlement and crossroads, later a Western Roman capital. Now modern Milan, Italy.
A Classical settlement, probably the Pylos of Thucydides, on the Koryphasion promontory, (modern Akr. Koryphasiou in Messenia) in the Peloponnese.
A Final Bronze Age settlement of four to five hectares in South Etruria.
A Gallo-Roman city and the capital of the Lingones.
A Gallo-Roman pottery manufacturing center produdcing white clay statuettes as well as terra sigillata.
A Gallo-Roman sanctuary identified in the 1960s at La Cavée du Moulin near Hanches in the Eure-et-Loir department of France.
A Gallo-Roman settlement and associated necropolis were discovered in the vicinity of the modern Belgian village of Pommerœul in the 1970s.
A Gallo-Roman settlement founded on a Celtic oppidum

A Gallo-Roman settlement that persisted until the fourth century of the modern era at modern La Chapelle-des-Fougeretz. Known since the 20th century, rescue excavations ahead of a housing development on the southwest edge of the modern town were conducted in 2022 and revealed a sanctuary of Mars, a civic bath complex, and a late-antique necropolis. The site's ancient name(s) are unknown.
A Gallo-Roman vicus covering ca. 10 ha.

A Gallo-Roman vicus in the area of modern Rumst in Belgium. Stray finds and unsystematic excavation in the 19th century pointed to specific locations for the civic center at Molenveld and necropolis at Kattenberg. There is epigraphic evidence for Roman riverine military activity in the area.
A Graeco-Roman town of Crete located 14 km E of Rethymno.
A Greek and Roman port, terminus of the Via Appia.

A Greek city at the easternmost point of the Italian peninsula that sided against Rome in both the Pyrrhic and Hannibalic wars. In the time of the Roman Empire the city was located in the province of Calabria and was an embarkation point for ships leaving for Apollonia across the Adriatic Sea.
A Greek city established by Miletos ca. 540 B.C. on the site of an earlier second millennium B.C. settlement.
A Greek city in Thrace located on the east bank of the Strymon river, Amphipolis was originally founded as an Athenian colony.
A Greek city located on the eastern side of the Hellespont.

A Greek city of ancient Caria that was part of the Dorian Hexapolis, was initially probably located at modern Burgaz in south-western Asia Minor on the Datça peninsula (Knidia) in Turkey. In the late fourth century BCE, the political center of the peninsula moved from the site at Burgaz to the site at Tekir, retaining the its ancient name. The Burgaz site is often referred to as "Old Cnidus" or "Palaia Knidos" in recognition of this change.

A Greek colonial city founded by Naxians in 729 B.C., Leontini was reduced by Hippocrates of Gela in 498 B.C. Following the Sicilian Expedition, the city became subject to Syracuse. In Roman times, it may have been of little importance and was destroyed by the Saracens in A.D. 848.
A Greek colonial city founded in 706 B.C.
A Greek colonial city located on the southern coast of Sicily, Selinus was said to have been founded as a colony of the city of Megara Hyblaia.
A Greek colony and long-time settlement on the island of the same name, located to the north of Sicily in the Tyrrhenian Sea. Modern Lipari.
A Greek colony and port on the west coast of the Black Sea, modern Mangalia in Romania.
A Greek colony founded by Miletus in the sixth century BC.
A Greek colony founded in Sicily ca. 598 B.C., Acrillae was an important economic center. In 213 B.C., the Roman consul M. Claudius Marcellus fought an engagement against the Syracusans there.
A Greek colony of Sicily founded by Rhodians and Cretans ca. 688 B.C. The oikists were the Rhodian Antiphemos and the Cretan Entimos.
A Greek settlement on the coast of the Sea of Azov.
A Greek trading settlement in northeastern Spain founded by the Rhodians.

A Hellenistic and Roman settlement that eventually prospered under the Byzantine Empire, Amorion began minting its own coins in the second century BCE. Its decline comes following a sacking in the ninth century at the hands of Caliph Al-Mu'tasim.
A Hellenistic and Roman site located on the right bank of the Aous river with a defensive circuit of ca. 2 km.
A Hellenistic city founded under either King Tigranes I, or his son and successor King Tigranes the Great.
A Hellenistic fort located on the Kainys promontory (modern Punta del Pezzo) in southern Italy.
A Hellenistic fortification and tower in southeastern Naxos.
A Hellenistic settlement with Illyrian antecedents located at modern Stobreč in Croatia. The city flourished into late antiquity.
A Hellenistic village that later became a key site during the Great Jewish Revolt.

A Hellenistic-and-Roman-era site, sometimes locally referred to as Palaiokastro, on the northwest coast of Cyprus, west of the modern village of Ag. Eirini. Archaeological investigation also produced evidence of Bronze Age habitation here. The historical site is possibly to be identified with the attested name Melabron.

A Hernican hill town that formed part of a sixth-century B.C. defensive league against Volscian and Samnite aggression and allied itself to Tarquinius Superbus. Rome eventually took Aletrium in 306 B.C.; by the first century B.C., the town was a Roman municipium.
A Hernican town along the Via Latina that the Romans captured in 364 B.C. Later in the Republican period (after 195 B.C.), the city received Roman municipal status.

A Ibero-Roman fortified settlement with substantial archaeological remains stretching into the Middle Ages. The site of Ategua is located near an abandoned farmstead called Cortijo de Teba la Vieja in the area of modern Santa Cruz, approximately 24 kilometers to the southeast of Cordoba in Spain.
A Judean, Edomite, and later Hellenistic settlement. Destroyed ca. 40 BCE by the Parthians.
A Late Iron Age necropolis of Ligurian culture.
A Late Roman fortlet in Tunisia, known today as Ksar Tarcine.
A Latin center in the Monti Lepini that was already a Roman municipium by 211 B.C.
A Latin colony founded ca. 312 B.C. along the Via Latina. The site was sacked by Samnites (ca. 294 B.C.) and subsequently by Hannibal (212 B.C.). It received Roman municipal status in 90 B.C.
A Latin colony in south Etruria founded ca. 273 B.C.
A Latin settlement that became a Roman municipium.
A Lucanian settlement located on the river Tanagro, now Atena Lucana.
A Lycian settlement located near modern Çukurbağ.
A Minoan palace complex and settlement on Crete, finally abandoned ca. 1200 BCE. The original toponym is unknown, and the modern name is derived from stone vessels found at the site.
A Numidian site that eventually became a Roman colony in the second century A.D.
A Phoenician and Roman town in Spain located on the Bay of Gibraltar. The site played a strategic role in the Punic Wars, and was given the rights of a Latin colony in 171 BC.
A Phoenician, Carthaginian, and Roman center in northeast Sardinia.
A Phoenician–Punic and later Roman settlement in southwestern Sardinia, Monte Sirai also has evidence for nuragic settlement during the second millennium BC.
A Praedium or estate located in Etruria near Siena; the modern Galognano.
A Pre-Roman settlement located north of the Étang de Thau.
A Ptolemaic city and temple built by Ptolemy II between 280 and 270 BC.
A Ptolemaic foundation in northern Jordan that eventually became part of the Decapolis.
A Punic center located west of Carthage.
A Punic city of northeastern Tunisia, near Cape Bon, abandoned ca. 250 BC (cited: BAtlas 32 H3 Kerkouane)
A Roman and Late Antique settlement on the island of Pseira marked in BAtlas after Myers 1992.

A Roman and Late-antique fort and quarry at Mons Claudianus (modern Jabal Faţīrah) and in the associated Deir Wadi Umm Hussein in Egypt's eastern desert. It is often referred to in scholarly literature and the press simply as "Mons Claudianus" because of its location. Excavations at the site are notable in part for the recovery of a large textual archive that details the operations and daily life of soldiers and workers at the site.
A Roman army camp on the Danube River in Noricum; after the first century CE Carnuntum served as the capital of Upper Pannonia.
A Roman auxiliary fort at present day Ribchester
A Roman auxiliary fort at present-day Castleshaw.
A Roman auxiliary fort at present-day Doncaster.
A Roman auxiliary fort in Wales.
A Roman auxiliary fort on the Danube river at modern Ram (Serbia). It was reduced in size by the time of Diocletian and then renovated and expanded under Justinian.
A Roman auxiliary fort with associated vicus and port at modern Vleuten-De Meern in the Dutch province of Utrecht.
A Roman auxiliary fort.
A Roman auxiliary fort. Limited excavations in 1969 suggested a construction date of ca. A.D. 83 with abandonment ca. 87.
A Roman border fort and associated vicus located near the modern German town of Schramberg.
A Roman camp and statio on the right bank of the Danube River that was the station of Cohors II Flavia Brittonum equitata and Cohors II Mattiacorum.
A Roman camp located in the middle of the modern village of Zăvoi in Romania. The site may be associated with a road station known as Acmonia/Augmonia/Agnavi(a)e in ancient sources.

A Roman camp with baths and associated settlement were identified at modern Souk El Arbaa in Morocco in the late 19th and 20th centuries on high ground occupied by a qubba called "Sidi Aïssa". Although ancient structures and settlement extent identified previously are not visible in modern satellite imagery, the site -- bisected by a rail line predating 1941 and occupied by a cemetery and more recent structures -- can still be correlated closely with previously published photographs and plans. Recent scholarly opinion diverges from that reflected in the Barrington Atlas to lean toward identifying this site with ancient (Vo)psiciana (q.v.), attested by Ptolemy, the Antonine Itinerary, and the Ravenna Cosmographer.

A Roman castellum, located adjacent to the ancient settlement of Aporidos Come and the Aulutrene lake (modern Çapalı/Karakuyu in Turkey's Afyonkarahisar province). An initial (temporary?) camp on/near the location may have been established as early as the second century BC; however, archaeological and epigraphic evidence point to a small, stone-built installation with associated garrison, possibly during the Severan period that was later expanded in Byzantine times. The stone structure, at the modern town of Eldere, was heavily quarried and built over by the 1980s.
A Roman castrum of the limes Arabicus. In the fourth century, Legio IV Martia was stationed here.
A Roman city located in the province of Mauretania Tingitana, along the road from Tingi to Sala. The city is mentioned by Ptolemy, the Antonine Itinerary, and the Geographer of Ravenna.
A Roman city of Baetica that was perhaps founded by the Carthaginians in the fifth century BC. Modern Malaga, on the Mediterranean coast of Spain.
A Roman city on the Via Aemilia.

A Roman city with Turdetanian origins. It is cited on both the Antonine Itinerary and the Vicarello goblets. Based on these itineraries it is to be located between Ugia (Torre Alocaz, Utrera) and Hispalis (Seville), near the banks of the Lacus Ligustinus.
A Roman city with likely Celtic roots and a long, subsequent architectural history, the historic center of modern Évora in Portugal was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1986.
A Roman city, founded by Claudius, that was the capital of Noricum.
A Roman colonia in western Sardinia.

A Roman colonial town founded in the Aurès Mountains of Algeria by the Emperor Trajan around AD 100. The city's full name was Colonia Marciana Ulpia Traiana Thamugadi. Trajan named the city in commemoration of his mother Marcia, eldest sister Ulpia Marciana, and father Marcus Ulpius Traianus.
A Roman colony that was established in the third or second century B.C., Heba lay near modern Magliano. Funerary evidence indicates previous Etruscan occupation at the site.
A Roman encampment located along the road from Lederata to Tibiscum, on the left bank of Bîrzava river.
A Roman fort and associated settlement (vicus) known today as Henchir Bessariani. It is located southwest of modern Negrine in Algeria.
A Roman fort and associated structures at modern Stolniceni, Romania. An indigenous settlement was likely located a few kilometers to the north.
A Roman fort and associated vicus at modern Greta Bridge (UK).
A Roman fort and tower in the modern French commune of St-Gemmes-le-Robert (Pays de la Loire).
A Roman fort and town located between Deva Victrix (Chester) and Viroconium Cornoviorum (Wroxeter).
A Roman fort associated with the Antonine Wall at modern day Carriden House. It does not lie on the Wall itself, but rather is 1.3 km to the south east of the Wall's eastern terminus at Bridgeness.
A Roman fort at Bowness on Solway on the Stanegate.
A Roman fort at modern Brougham in the United Kingdom (sometimes called Brougham Castle Roman Fort).
A Roman fort at modern-day Burrow Walls, probably to be identified with the ancient toponym "Magis".
A Roman fort at present day Caernarvon. The first Roman fort was built under Agricola ca. A.D. 77 and the site was occupied by Romans until ca. 338.
A Roman fort at present-day Bainbridge.
A Roman fort at present-day Birrens, cited: BAtlas 9 D5 Blatobulgium
A Roman fort at present-day Caersws, Wales.
A Roman fort at present-day Chester-le-Street.
A Roman fort at present-day Ebchester.
A Roman fort at present-day Hardknott.
A Roman fort at present-day High Rochester.
A Roman fort at present-day Kirkby Thore.
A Roman fort at present-day Lanchester.
A Roman fort at present-day Maryport. Part of Cumbrian coastal defenses.
A Roman fort at present-day Moresby that was a part of the Cumbrian coastal defenses.
A Roman fort at present-day Old Carlisle.
A Roman fort at present-day Papcastle, cited: BAtlas 9 D6 Derventio
A Roman fort at present-day Risingham.
A Roman fort at present-day South Shields.
A Roman fort at present-day Whitley Castle.
A Roman fort in Newton Kyme, England.
A Roman fort in Pannonia Superior east of Brigetio that was the base of the cohors V Callaecorum Lucensium.
A Roman fort in Scotland built ca. A.D. 83 that served as a supply base.
A Roman fort in Scotland.

A Roman fort is thought to have been established at Lindinis (modern Ilchester) ca. 60 CE. The site protected the crossing of the Fosse Way over the River Yeo. The settlement developed in phases from the first to the fourth centuries CE. It was eventually one of only two known settlements with a stone wall in the territory of the Durotriges. The inhabitants of the town seem to have been reasonably wealthy, as a number of domestic complexes have fine mosaic pavements.

A Roman fort located along the Roman road from Brougham to Ravenglass. The previous association with Ambleside is now in doubt since the discovery of a diploma at Ravenglass in 1995, which plausibly links Itunocelum with Ravenglass, and consequently making Ambleside more likely to be identified with *Glannoventa.
A Roman fort located at modern Ajdovščina in Slovenia.

A Roman fort located in and around the modern village of Pumsaint in Wales, it is probably the "Louentinon" mentioned by Ptolemy. The Latinate form "Luentinum" is common in the literature but is not attested by any ancient source.

A Roman fort north of Hadrian's Wall. BAtlas, following Rivet, identified it with "Fanum Cocidi", a toponym that is known only from the Ravenna Cosmographer. Durham rejects this view and would place F. "near the mouth of the river Annan".
A Roman fort occupied ca. 150-260 CE.
A Roman fort of Hadrian's Wall, located between Banna (Birdoswald) to the east and Uxelodunum (Stanwix) to the west. It lies approximately 11 km west of Birdoswald and commands the Cambeck Valley.
A Roman fort of the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes, Böhming is located in the Eichstätt district of Bavaria. The fort was destroyed in the late third century CE.
A Roman fort of the first and second centuries A.D. at present day Melandra Castle.
A Roman fort of the first and second century AD in Wales.
A Roman fort on Hadrian's Wall, cited: BAtlas 9 D6 ‘Congavata’
A Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
A Roman fort on the German Limes.
A Roman fort on the Pannonian Limes, at modern Szentendre in Hungary.
A Roman fort on the Raetian limes, located in what is now Aalen in the modern German state of Baden-Württemberg. It was garrisoned by the Ala II Flavia Miliaria Pia Fidelis.
A Roman fort on the island of Alderney in the English Channel. Its ancient name is unknown.
A Roman fort on the island of Lesbos.
A Roman fort probably to be equated with the site at present-day Castledykes.
A Roman fort that is probably to be identified with modern-day Dalginross.

A Roman fort was established near the present-day village of Leintwardine ca. 70 CE. The fort was situated close to the confluence of the river Clun with the river Teme, along the Roman road now known as "Watling Street West".
A Roman fort with associated vicus located at modern Schirenhof in the German municipality of Schwäbisch Gmünd, Baden-Württemberg.
A Roman fort, cited: BAtlas 9 F6 Piercebridge

A Roman fort, likely constructed and later abandoned during the first century CE, possibly with an associated mansio. Easter Happrew is located in the modern parish of Stobo in Scotland. It may correspond to Karbantorigon, which is listed by Ptolemy.
A Roman fort, most likely called Verbeia, at modern-day Ilkley in the U.K.

A Roman fortification located about a kilometer south of the modern German village of Kneblinghausen that was excavated at the beginning of the 20th century and is thought to date to the early period of Roman military engagement in the region.
A Roman fortification on the Oude Rijn, Praetorium Agrippinae was likely established under Caius ca. AD 39 or 40.
A Roman fortlet in Tripolitana (modern Ksar Ghilane in Tunisia).
A Roman funerary monument located at modern Vilablareix, southwest of Girona, in Catalonia.
A Roman garrison town located near the Chaboras that was later renamed Theodosiopolis.
A Roman industrial site of the late first century A.D. located at the crossing of the river Mersey.
A Roman legionary base first established ca. AD 15.
A Roman legionary camp, approximately dating to the years 4-6 CE, located at modern Anreppen, Stadt Delbrück (Germany).

A Roman legionary encampment (castrum) associated with the Legio X Gemina that later developed into a Roman town. The site is located in the Vidriales valley in the province of Zamora (Castilla y Leon).
A Roman limes fortress located in Mesopotamia, along the Khabur river, near the point where it flows into the Euphrates.
A Roman maritime community that may derive its name from a local sanctuary of Venus, Portus Veneris served as the base of the Byzantine fleet until it was destroyed in A.D. 643.
A Roman military outpost during the Roman invasion of the Dora Baltea ca. 100 B.C., Eporedia was assigned to Regio XI.
A Roman military site in Jordan, it was bulldozed out of existence between 2013 and 2017.
A Roman mining center located in the Iglesiente region of Sardinia. The Roman settlement succeeded an earlier nuragic village.
A Roman municipal center and port.
A Roman municipium founded in 87 BC after the Social War, Iuvanum sits on the site of a pre-existing Samnite settlement that occupies an upland plateau.
A Roman municipium of the first century A.D.
A Roman municipium with an orthogonal plan.
A Roman pottery production center located at Westerndorf St Peter in south Bavaria.
A Roman road station (mansio) on the Via Nova Traiana. Modern Khirbet es-Samra in Jordan.
A Roman seaside community on the Bay of Naples that included thermal springs.
A Roman settlement along the Via Domitia.
A Roman settlement and municipium near the Sava river, on the location of the modern village of Šćitarjevo, Croatia, south of Zagreb, near Velika Gorica.
A Roman settlement at Petinesca replaced a Celtic oppidum located on the plateau of the Jensberg. The site was located along the military highway from Aventicum to Salodurum.

A Roman settlement built atop an earlier Umbrian one on a western foothill of the Apennines, Asisium received municipal status and was assigned to the Tribus Sergia. Totila destroyed most of the city in A.D. 545.
A Roman settlement established in the second century A.D. as the legionary base of Legio III Augusta.
A Roman settlement in Spain
A Roman settlement located at modern Freixo in Portugal.

A Roman settlement located immediately to the southeast of modern Didymoteicho, Greece, Plotinopolis was founded by the Roman emperor Trajan in honor of his wife, Plotina. Roman-era material culture has been identified at the site, beginning with chance finds in the 1960s and continuing through subsequent scientific excavation.
A Roman settlement located southwest of modern St Albans, Hertfordshire, England.
A Roman settlement on the coast of Liguria.
A Roman signal station/fortlet near Ravenscar on the Yorkshire coast.
A Roman signal station/fortlet of the Yorkshire coast, England.
A Roman signal station/fortlet on the Yorkshire coast, England
A Roman site in modern Jordan, known today as ‘Ayn Gharandal. It includes remains of a late Roman fort and bathhouse.
A Roman site with evidence for a series of ditched enclosures of the first century.
A Roman to Late Antique settlement with substantial remains of public religious buildings, including a large temple, residential areas, tombs, and three churches.
A Roman town and fort at present-day Corbridge.
A Roman town where the emperor Vespasian was born in A.D. 9.
A Roman vexillation fort of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes.

A Roman vexillation fortress of the first century A.D. was located at Longthorpe near Peterborough. The site was first identified via crop marks in 1961 and some excavations were carried out between 1967 and 1971. Nothing of the site is now visible as it has been consumed by a golf course. The fort had two phases: the first phase of 11 ha (27 acres) dates as early as A.D. 44-48 (definitely occupied by 61-62. A contracted phase of 4.5 ha (11 acres) followed later.
A Roman vicus on the Nahe river.
A Roman vicus, corresponding to the modern Frankfurt am Main-Heddernheim in Germany.

A Roman-era camp with bath and associated hot springs in modern Algeria's Charef district. The site, now built over by a modern resort hotel complex, was located where the modern road between Charef and Djelfa crosses the Oued el Hadjia. In 2026, OpenStreetMap records the local post office as having the name "El Hammam".
A Roman-era fort and associated well at Deir Umm Deheis in modern Egypt's Eastern Desert.

A Roman-period hilltop site, partially excavated in the 20th century, that lies just west of the modern Spanish village of El Chuche in the municipal district of Benahadux, Almeria. It is probably to be associated with the attested Roman name "Urci". The archaeological record of human habitation on and near the site stretches back to the Chalcolithic.
A Sabine town that was later known as a mansio on the course of the Via Salaria.
A Sabine town, 30 km east-north-east of Rome, Tibur was the seat of the Tiburtine Sibyl.
A Samnite settlement at the margins of Campania.
A Samnite settlement occupying a strategic location in the valley of the Sangro river.
A Samnite town that eventually became a Roman municipium of the tribus Falerna ca. 89 B.C.
A Sikel center located on a calcareous hill (560 m). There is evidence of rock-cut chamber tombs dating to the archaic period.
A Sumerian city-state.
A Tyrrhenian coastal port opposite Elba. Modern Piombino.
A Urartian settlement on a hill overlooking the Euphrates River
A Volscian center that Rome reportedly destroyed in the late fourth century B.C.
A Volscian hilltop settlement that became a Roman colony in 312 B.C.
A Volscian settlement of the fifth century B.C. that became a Latin colony in 382 B.C.

A ancient settlement in western Anatolia, ca. 8 km west of the modern town of Milas in the Muğla Province. Remains of the ancient settlement are located under and around the modern village of Damlıboğaz.
A capital town founded by Carthaginians.
A celtiberian and subsequent Roman settlement at modern Ciudad Rodrigo in Salamanca, Spain.

A center for Numidian royalty, Bulla Regia first became an oppidum liberum in the reign of Augustus and then a colony under Hadrian. The site, which boasts significant archaeological remains, lies in modern Tunisia, about 5km north of the modern city of Jendouba. The site was reportedly known in the 19th century as Hammam-Darradji. Today, a small modern settlement named Aïn Babouch abuts the site (not to be confused with Babouch, which lies further north along the border with Algeria).
A center of the Elymian people in northwestern Sicily.
A center of the Messapii in Apulia.
A center of the ancient Daunians, Canusium became allied to Rome in 318 B.C. It received municipal status in 88 B.C.
A chief settlement of the Peligni that was ravaged by the Carthaginians during the Second Punic War.
A city and capital of Ancient Egypt that remained an important center for most of Egyptian history.
A city at the former mouth of the Achelous river.
A city at the mouth of the Axius river.
A city founded by Corinth in the seventh century B.C. on the gulf of Ambracia.
A city founded by Ptolemy I Soter as the capital of Upper Egypt.
A city founded by Seleucus Nicator between 296 and 280 BC.

A city founded ca. 300 BC by Seleucus I Nicator, a successor of Alexander the Great. Antioch was a great trading center and numbered as one of the four cities of the Syrian tetrapolis. Justinian I renamed the city 'Theoupolis' in the sixth century AD.
A city founded in 627 B.C. by colonists from Corinth and Kerkyra.
A city founded in the second century B.C. at the junction of the Via Postumia and Via Aemilia Scauri which merged to become the Via Julia Augusta.
A city in Achaea Phthiotis, the mythical home of Protesilaos. It had been absorbed into Thebai Phthiotides by the 3rd century BC.
A city in Armenia, founded by Tigranes II as capital of his kingdom in the first half of the 1st century BC.
A city in Armenia, probably founded by Arsames in the early second century BCE, perhaps at the site of modern Haraba (now under the Keban Dam Lake)
A city in Persis founded or re-founded by Antiochos I Soter, perhaps located at Bushahr, Rishahr, or Tawwaj.
A city in Phrygia named after its legendary founder, king Midas.
A city in Sittakene and/or Babylonia, located on the Silla River.
A city in Spain founded in 206 B.C. by Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus as a site at which to settle Roman soldiers wounded in the Battle of Ilipa.
A city located in the northern part of the ancient Krokian plain, near modern Akitsi/Mikrothivai.
A city located on the Tigris, where it split into two streams, in the region of Mesene, founded by Antiochos I.
A city located on the west coast of Acarnania. The southwestern portion of the walled city underlies modern Kandila.
A city of Africa Proconsularis, Simitthu is especially noted for its marble quarries.
A city of Arcadia and home of the cult of Despoina
A city of Bruttium, located south of the Mataurus river at the border with Rhegium.
A city of Campania located between Capua and Neapolis.
A city of Campania with Osco-Etruscan origins that became a Roman colony in 197 B.C.
A city of Cilicia with Hittite origins, Hierapolis/Kastabala later became part of the Cilician satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire and, later, part of the Roman empire.
A city of Cisalpine Gaul located in the territory of the Insubres.
A city of Corsica with significant pre-historic, Greek, Etruscan, and Roman phases.
A city of Gallia Belgica located on the Somme that is mentioned in Caesar's commentaries.
A city of Latium Adjectum established as a Latin colony ca. 494 B.C.
A city of Mysia located on the Hellespont.

A city of Phocis on the Boeotian frontier. Substantive remains of the ancient walled city are visible on the height immediately south of modern Hagios Vlasios (Municipality of Livadia, Boeotia, Greece).

A city of Pisidia, the site of Prostanna is located near modern Eğridir in Turkey in a saddle between the peak of Sivri Tepe and the main body of Davras Daği. Prostanna is mentioned in two literary sources (Ptolemy 5.5.7 and a listing of of bishops attending the Council of Constantinople in 381). The name is also attested in an inscription from Delos that dates ca. 113 B.C.
A city of Samnium located between Capua and Beneventum. In 321 B.C., the Samnites under C. Pontius encamped there before defeating the Romans at the Battle of the Caudine Forks.
A city of Tyrrhenian Etruria that came under Roman control in 280 B.C.; the Latin colony of Cosa was established nearby in 273 B.C.
A city of Upper Egypt, Oxyrhynchus/Pemje is particularly well known as an archaeological site that has produced important papyrus manuscripts of ancient texts.

A city of ancient Umbrian and Etruscan origin, Perusia aided Rome during the Second Punic War but was sieged and reduced by Octavian in the first century B.C. during campaigns against Lucius Antonius. It was rebuilt by Augustus and became Colonia Vibia Augusta Perusia quite late, in A.D. 251-3, under Trebonianus Gallus.
A city of northern Adriatic Italy that served as the capital of the Western Roman Empire from A.D. 402 until 476.
A city of northern Apulia.
A city of northern Attika at the boundary of Boeotia, Eleutherai is one of the best preserved ancient fortresses in Attica.
A city of northern Greece founded by Cassander of Macedon ca. 315 BCE; an important center of the Roman and Late Antique worlds.
A city of southeast Boeotia mentioned by Homer.
A city of southeastern Crete, mentioned by Strabo. It may be associated with the "Kastellos" at modern Kalamafka.
A city of the Aequiculi located in the valley of the Salto river.
A city of the Carricini Samnites. Its site was surveyed and partially excavated in the 19th and 20th centuries in the vicinity of modern Piano La Roma, a locality to the northwest of modern Casoli.
A city of the Decapolis in northern Jordan.
A city of the Peucetii that came under Roman control in the third century BCE.

A city of the Po Plain with important cultural phases related to Etruscan, Celtic, and Roman culture. Important evidence for the Iron Age Villanovan culture has been found in Bononia and its vicinity. The Romans established a Latin colony of ca. 3000 settlers at Bononia in 189 BC. After changing hands several times following the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Bologna became an important Medieval center.
A city of the Rhodian Peraea located close to the Gulf of Kos.
A city of the Samnites that, according to Livy, was captured by the Romans in Republican times. Probably at or in the vicinity of modern Roccavecchia di Pratella in Italy.
A city of the Siculi on the northern coast of Sicily.
A city of the Troad in the territory of Lampsacus that Strabo describes as being "rich in vines".
A city of the indigenous Sikels, Centuripae allied itself with Athens during the expedition against Syracuse.
A city of the west bank of the Nile, Lykopolis/Siout was the capital of the Thirteenth Nome of Upper Egypt (Lycopolites Nome) around 3100 B.C.
A city on the Adriatic coast of Dalmatia with a protected harbor.

A city settled in an area subjugated by Rome during the fourth century B.C. The local populace rebelled against Rome after the defeat at Cannae (216 B.C.), however the defeat of the Carthaginians eventually led to Potentia's reincorporation into the Roman sphere.
A city situated on the Tyrrhenian seaboard and likely of Etruscan origin. Its early nature was that of a mercantile center. The city became a Roman colony in 89 B.C.
A city with an extensive circuit wall, temple, theater, and agora.

A city with its origins in a Phoenician settlement of the seventh century BC, Caralis comes under Roman control in 238 BC during the Punic Wars. Florus refers to it as urbs urbinum, or capital of Sardinia
A city-state of ancient Achaea that numbered as one of the 12 Achaean cities. The city was located 30 stades from Rhypae, and 40 stades from Helice.
A classical deme of Attica, located at modern Trachones / Ano Kalamaki. The area has been continuously exploited or inhabited by humans since at least the Neolithic period.
A cluster of mines and associated late-antique settlement at Bir Umm Fawakhir in Egypt's Eastern Desert.
A coastal city of Dalmatia.
A coastal deme of the tribe Aigeis, in Attica, located on the eastern shore north of Brauron. The site was known in antiquity for its sanctuary dedicated to Artemis Tauropolos.
A coastal deme of the tribe Antiochis in Attika, located on Anavyssos Bay.

A coastal settlement founded by Greeks, Tyritake is located about 11 km south of Kerch. The city's foundation dates to the middle of the sixth century BCE, although a Late Bronze Age settlement may have preceded the Greek colonial foundation. The city became a part of the Bosporan state and flourished until the late fourth century CE. It is noted for its circuit of fortification walls.
A coastal settlement of Phoenicia, now Tel Dor, to the south of Haifa.
A coastal town of Paphlagonia.
A coastal village on the island of Euboea known especially for rich Bronze Age and Iron Age material.
A colony founded by Teos on the Gulf of Taman ca. 540 BC.
A colony of Athens founded c. 445 BC.
A colony of Miletus that eventually came to be part of the kingdom of Pontus.
A colony on the north shore of Sicily founded in 649/8 BC by the Myletidai.

A complex of Roman military structures was established and upgraded between the first and third centuries CE on the banks of the Neckar River in Germany where modern Heidelberg now stands. Forts, bridges, roads, and manufacturing facilities with attendant burials and inscriptions have been excavated.

A deme located to the east of Mt. Hymettus. The site is located on the eastern outskirts of modern Liopesi. The epithet "Lower" ("Hypenerthen") distinguished it from the small Upper Paiania, but the two formed a single entity for many purposes.
A deme of Attica located near Pousi Kaloyerou.
A deme of ancient Attica that belonged to the phyle of Acamantis.
A deme of ancient Attica that was located in the center of Athens to the northeast of the Dipylon Gate.

A famous Euboean spa city in the Hellenistic and Roman periods, located at modern Loutra Aidepsou. The polis' original location may have been 3-4 km north in the area of a modern town that carries the modern name Aidepsos (previously Lipso).

A first- through tenth-century CE settlement located on the right bank of the Euphrates River in Syria's Aleppo Governorate, the site of Dibsi Faraj was excavated in the 1970s ahead of the Tabqa Dam project which eventually inundated the area. The excavations were jointly organized by Dumbarton Oaks and the University of Michigan under Richard Harper, following initial work by the Syrian culture ministry. The site was shown to be a heavily fortified one with Roman and Byzantine phases. It came to be abandoned after ca. 859 CE.
A fort abutting the Anastasian Wall, 5km west of Çiftlikköy Merkez and 6km northeast of Gümüşpınar in Turkey.
A fort and associated settlement on the Koroneia peninsula on the east coast of Attica.
A fort and associated vicus on Hadrian's Wall.

A fort and vicus located on the Rhine near the southwest end of Lake Constance. A military outpost was created here in the early first century. The site was likely abandoned at the beginning of the fifth century.
A fort constructed ca. 11 BC to protect a wooden bridge built to span the Rhine river.
A fort located at the frontier between Attica and Boeotia, on the slopes of Mt. Cithaeron.
A fort on Hadrian's Wall known today as Halton Chesters.
A fort on Hadrian's Wall.
A fort on the Antonine Wall at Cadder.
A fort or tower associated with the Anastasian Wall in Thrace.
A fort south of Hadrian's Wall and findspot of the Vindolanda Tablets. The earliest phases of Roman occupation date ca. 80 CE. Much of the fort was rebuilt ca. 300 CE.
A fortified Etruscan settlement on Ilva.
A fortified Medieval site in the Maremma region of Italy with evidence for earlier fortified centers.
A fortified Mycenaean center in the Argolid that flourished between 1400 and 1200 B.C.
A fortified Roman and Medieval site with occupation beginning from the fourth millennium B.C.
A fortified Roman settlement located 7 km south of the city of Keszthely, Hungary.
A fortified Roman town along the line of Watling Street.
A fortified acropolis known as Kastro Rogon and located near modern Nea Karasounta in Epirus, Greece has been identified as the likely site of ancient Bouchetion, a colony of Elis.

A fortified acropolis, discovered in 1989 on the Vigla hill south of the modern Greek town of Hagios Nikolaos (Plagia Community, Palairos Municipality). As yet unexcavated, monumental stone remains as well as pottery of the 5th/4th centuries BCE have been reported at the site. Some scholars have suggested that the attested city of Sollion could have been located here.
A fortified ancient Greek city located in southern Epirus.

A fortified ancient Roman settlement noted by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas) in the vicinity of contemporary "Koudiat Adjela". The fragmentary ancient name was provided by an inscription discovered in 1930 at "Mechta Sidi-Hassem," which has also been reported as "Douar Boutara". The location should lie within a kilometer of the BAtlas coordinates: a point to the northwest of modern Ksar El Abtal and immediately north of Douar Nouaoura in Algeria's Setif Wilaya.
A fortified ancient hilltop, Ferrazzano is usually identified as a Samnite site.
A fortified ancient settlement near modern Lentini. It has been associated with the area of Monte San Basilio.
A fortified area of indeterminate chronology located on Mount Merenda in Attica.
A fortified center located in the comune of Ciorlano.
A fortified center of Lucania founded in the fifth century B.C. or earlier, Pomarico Vecchio was influenced by its close contacts with the Greek cities of Magna Graecia.
A fortified coastal site on the Adriatic Sea with a long history of occupation stretching from the Bronze Age (fifteenth to eleventh centuries BC) to the Middle Ages.
A fortified hilltop palace in Jordan located southeast of the mouth of the Jordan river on the eastern side of the Dead Sea.
A fortified hilltop settlement overlooking the Soulima Valley in northern Messenia. Dorion appears in the Catalogue of Ships in Homer's Iliad.
A fortified outpost (phrourion) of the city of Velia/Elea.
A fortified port located on the Gulf of Corinth near Alepokhori.
A fortified settlement located just before the First Cataract of the Nile. During the Second Intermediate Period, Elephantine marked the southern border of Egypt.

A fortified settlement, probably constructed in the Hellenistic period, located south of the modern Greek village of Asfaka (Souli municipality, Epirus). An extensive, elite residence was built inside the fortification in early Roman times. The modern chapel of Ag. Donatos, which incorporates spolia from a Hellenistic structure, was built on part of the lower terrace of the ancient site.
A fortified site on the Via Appia dating to the Republican period.
A fortified tower on high ground west of modern Thymonia bay on the south coast of the Aegean island of Thasos.
A fortified town located some 6 km from Falerii Veteres and established by the ancient Romans ca. 241 B.C.
A fortified town of Paphlagonia on the Halys river, Pimolisa had been destroyed by Strabo's time. The district retained a memory of its name, however.
A fortress built by Dionysius the Elder 9 km west of Syracuse, in the modern hamlet of Belvedere (Sicily).
A fortress in Armenia Minor on the river Euphrates, some 75 Roman miles from Zimara.
A fortress of the Galatian Tolistobogii, the site of the palace and family tombs of the first century BC ruler Deiotarus.
A fortress of the ancient Corinthia captured by Agesilaus II of Sparta in 390 B.C.

A harbor city on the Black Sea, Polemonion/Side was founded in the region of Sidene (Pontus) by either Polemon I or Polemon II of Pontus. Following the Roman annexation of the Pontic kingdom in the 60s CE, the city's importance declined substantially.
A harbor settlement (in the vicinity of modern El Kantara) in the southern part of the Tunisian island of Djerba (ancient Meninx/Lotophagitis/Girba).
A harbor settlement on the island of the same name.

A hill located in the northern part of the modern Basilicata province of Italy. In addition to a prominent Norman castle, archaeological survey indicates human activity stretching back to the Bronze Age.

A key junction between roads north (towards Hattusa and the Lykos River valley), south (towards Mazaka), east (towards the upper Halys River), and west (towards Ankyra), it was inhabited from the fourth millennium BCE. Greek and Roman writers mention it as the main settlement of the Galatian tribe of the Trocmi.
A large Attic deme, located on the Gulf of Kotroni.
A large Bronze Age fortification of the Mycenaean civilization, Gla dates ca. 1300 B.C.

A large Roman or late Roman fortress that was at least partly maintained into the medieval period. Known today as Rabat Kalesi, it is located to the northeast of the village of Hisaraltı in modern Turkey.
A large ancient settlement located in the vicinity of modern Naix-aux-Forges and Saint-Armand-sur-Ornain in France. Excavations began in the 19th century and continued in the 20th.
A large archaeological site in modern Saudi Arabia's Najrān oasis: al-Ukhdūd.
A large settlement (vicus) of the Treveri, located at modern Arlon in Belgium.

A large settlement mound in modern Turkey's Elmalı basin where habitation from the Early Bronze Age through the Byzantine period has been documented. The city was known to Greek and Roman authors as Choma.

A large, fortified Phrygian settlement dating to the 7th/6th centuries BCE on modern Kerkenes Dağ in Turkey's Yozgat province. It is probably to be identified with a "Pteria" mentioned by Herodotus as the site of a battle between Cyrus and Croesus.

A largely overbuilt ancient village located in the West Bank. Archaeology indicates occupation as early as the 8th century BCE. Herodean fortifications, extended and occupied by Bar Kokhba's forces, were destroyed after a Roman siege in 135 CE.
A late Roman cavalry fort located in the modern German municipality of Isny im Allgäu (Baden-Württemberg).
A late Roman fort in Egypt's Kharga Oasis
A late Roman fort in Egypt's Kharga Oasis.
A late-Roman fortified settlement in Egypt's Kharga Oasis.
A likely Roman fort and possible Urartian fire temple at the modern village of Cengerli in the Refahiye district of Erzincan province, Turkey.
A major Etruscan city of North Etruria.
A major Greek city-state and the principal city of Attika. Modern Athens in Greece.

A major Sumerian city-state founded during the Ubaid period, ca. 3800 B.C. In archaeological terms, Ur is particularly well known for the lavish tombs of its Royal Cemetery, its massive Ziggurat. The site served as the capital of the Ur III dynasty.
A major ancient city in Ionia.
A major ancient settlement of Crete, located some 5 km southeast of Heraklion, Knossos was occupied from the Neolithic period to the time of the Roman Empire.
A major city of western Thessaly.
A major economic center in the Iberian peninsula, Emporiae (modern Empúries) had indigenous origins but would be the site of a large Greek colonial city.

A major settlement of Upper Mesopotamia from the Bronze Age onward. The earliest mentions of the site are found in the Ebla tablets (ca. 2300 B.C.). Notably, the location of the Battle of Carrhae between the Roman Republic and Parthian Empire in 53 B.C., which proved to be a devastating defeat for the Romans. Modern-day Ḥarrān, Turkey.
A major settlement, cited: BAtlas 32 D3 Numluli
A major settlement, cited: BAtlas 34 F2 Mascula Tiberia
A maritime city of Campania situated on the Phlegrean Peninsula. The settlement started as a Greek colony and became a Roman colony under the name Puteoli in 194 B.C.
A military port near Ravenna, established by Octavian by 12 B.C. as headquarters for the Roman fleet in the Adriatic Sea.
A minor settlement, cited: BAtlas 34 D2 Lamsorti
A minor settlement.

A modern village on the Aegean island of Lesbos. Remains of ancient houses have been noted in the area. Its modern name may preserve an ancient toponym preserved on a late-antique inscription. For these reasons, BAtlas followed Kontes 1978 in identifying it as the general area of a late antique settlement.
A mountainous area southwest of modern Marianopoli, inhabited since the sixth century B.C.

A multi-period complex in Egypt's eastern desert comprising a fort, settlement(s?), and production areas for gold-washing of quartz collected from the wadi alluvium. Most visible structures date to the Ptolemaic and Roman periods, but there is evidence for earlier activity during the New Kingdom period.

A multi-period series of Roman fortifications and associated vicus in the Noricum limes, grouped around the confluence of the modern Inn and Danube rivers (modern Passau and Innstadt in Germany). A Celtic oppidum preceded the Roman presence.
A multi-period settlement, with Bronze Age to Roman occupation, most notably the site of a large, Persian and Hellenistic administrative building.
A peak in south-central Sicily on which archaeological remains of a fortified settlement have been identified. The settlement's ancient name is unknown.
A place in Latium where tradition holds that Aeneas disembarked.
A place mentioned in the Antonine Itinerary (Pontibus). Scholars tentatively associate it with modern Ponches-Estruval in France's Somme department.
A place on the Tigris River mentioned by Ammianus Marcellinus.
A port at the mouth of the river Silarus that derived its name from Alburnus mons.
A port city founded by Aeolian settlers at the mouth of the River Avci.
A port city founded by colonists from Syracuse in 387 BC.
A port city of northern Boeotia located in the foothills of Mount Messapion on the Gulf of Euboea.
A port city on the Adriatic Sea (modern Pula in Croatia).

A port on the Aegean coast of Caria, south of Miletus, that provided a point of debarkation for travelers to Didyma, Panormos has been identified with the modern bay of Kovela Limanı. Although the ancient shoreline, harbor works, and presumed town have not been precisely located, an important archaic necropolis has been identified just east of the modern Turkish village of Mavişehir and archaeological survey in the area indicates a long and vibrant record of human occupation.
A port on the Tyrrhenian coast. In myth, the site was considered to be one of the stopping points of the hero Odysseus.
A port on the island of Ilva (modern Elba), so named based on the resting place of the Argonauts, according to Strabo.
A pre-Roman and Roman settlement on the island of Majorca. Its ruins are known as Pedret de Bóquer, which is located at the modern Port de Pollença. The original settlement dates ca. 1400 BC.
A pre-Roman and Roman site in southern Sardinia.
A pre-Roman and Romano-British settlement was located at Baldock along the Icknield Way.
A probable Samnite center, the Romans captured Aufidena in 298 BC. It only became a municipium after 49 B.C.
A production site for Gallo-Roman pottery occupied from the time of Augustus until the late second century AD.

A protohistoric site located near Metaponto in Italy, Incorata provides important evidence -- especially between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE -- for both indigenous Oenotrian and early Greek colonial physical culture in Italy.
A road station between Tarquimpol and Saverne.
A road station located along the road from Chalon-sur-Saone to Besançon.
A road station, possibly located at or en route to modern al-Ǧauf in Saudi Arabia, that epigraphic evidence from another location indicates was garrisoned by Roman soldiers during the Severan period.
A ruin by Pausanias' time, this ancient settlement was located near Megalopolis in Arcadia. Modern scholars think it probably was in the vicinity of modern Apiditsa.

A ruined Hellenistic wall-and-tower site (with subsequent additions) on the Xirokastrini hill between modern Kalloni and Parakoila on the island of Lesbos is possibly to be identified with the attested ancient settlement of Issa.

A rural location now in the modern Algerian municipal territory of Djouab (Médéa province) where Gsell and his correspondents (AAA, whence BAtlas) observed Roman ruins including a large building with columns that G. speculated might have been a church.
A sanctuary and grove of Feronia and an associated settlement located along the Via Tiberina in the territory of Capena.

A sanctuary of Thetis and/or settlement in the ancient territory of Pharsalus. Scholars have suggested various locations for the ancient site, including Ag. Athanassion at Kato Dasolophos (formerly Bekides) and the area of modern Thetidion (formerly Alchami).

A sanctuary of the Sequani at modern Villards-d'Heria in France. It is archaeologically represented by a two-part architectural complex comprising (1) north of the modern town the monumental "Pont des Arches", which supported a temple over a watercourse that supplied a large spa, and (2) at the nearby Lac-d'Antre, which supplied the majority of the water for the spa complex and also hosted additional temples along its shoreline. Plans in Vurpillot 2016 and Nouvel 2019.
A seaside settlement of ancient Thrace that was a colony of Mesembria. Some Romans seem to have referred to the site also as Templum Iovis.
A sequence of occupational phases at Haltern, Germany, results from the presence of the Roman military following from the earliest period of Roman occupation in the principate of Augustus.
A series of Roman forts and associated settlement (vicus), located where the modern Bavarian village of Künzing now stands.

A series of settlements and fortifications localized in and around the mound known today as Tel Afek/Râs el-'Ain in Israel. The mound itself is dominated today by the remains of an Ottoman fort, built on Crusader foundations, but an excavated Roman-era odeon can also be seen.
A settlement along Watling Street, roughly midway between Deva and Mamucium. i.e., located at the modern town of Northwich (Cheshire, England)
A settlement along the Via Laurentina that has yielded significant evidence for protohistoric occupation, including funereal evidence of the eighth and seventh centuries B.C.
A settlement and deme of Attica, probably located in the river valley north of Thorikos.
A settlement and harbor located in Ionia on Mt. Mykale in what is now western Turkey.
A settlement at the third milestone of the Via Ostiensis.

A settlement attested in ancient literature. Despite some suggestions to the contrary, scholarly consensus continues to identify Kalynda with an archaeological site at the modern village of Şerefler (formerly Kozpınar) in Turkey's Muğla province.
A settlement attested in ancient sources whose location can only be narrowed to the general area of modern Amra.
A settlement attested in ancient sources, that was probably located along the modern Ilias Çay in Turkey, downstream from the modern Yortanlı dam.
A settlement founded as a Roman municipium along the line of the Via Iulia Augusta by Julius Caesar ca. 50 BCE.

A settlement founded in Thrace to mark Trajan's victory in the Dacian Wars. It is located on the left bank of the Mesta river. Occupied through late antiquity, the site was destroyed by the seventh century and subsequently re-occupied by the late tenth century.
A settlement in Africa Proconsularis, mentioned in the Itinerarium Antonini and the Tabula Peutingeriana.

A settlement in Apulia that originated with the Samnites and Frentani and later came under Roman influence. During the Second Punic War, the Romans defeated Hannibal at Larinum. The settlement eventually gained Roman municipal status.
A settlement in Cappadocia located among "fairy chimney" rock formations.
A settlement in Etruria situated on the Via Aurelia between Centumcellae and Cosa according to the Antonine Itinerary.
A settlement in Thessaly mentioned by Herodotus, Kasthaneia is most likely at the site of modern Keramidi.
A settlement in east Crete in use from the Early Minoan period to the Late Minoan period and again in Roman times.
A settlement in the Roman province of Mauretania Caesariensis in North Africa.
A settlement in the interior of southern Corsica
A settlement in the territory of the Aedui mentioned by Caesar.
A settlement located at the Yonne-Vanne confluence in the territory of the Senones.
A settlement located at the juncture of the Jordan and Jezreel valleys, Scythopolis/Nysa had important Egyptian through Roman phases.
A settlement located in the border region between the ager Falernus and the ager Campanus, north of Capua.
A settlement located on the road between Damascus and Emesa.
A settlement mentioned in ancient sources whose precise location cannot be determined today. BAtlas offered two possible identifications: Phaine or Buraq.
A settlement mound located in western Iran near Malayer. The site has multiple phases, none of which date earlier than 800 BCE.
A settlement of Hispania Baetica in the territory of Castulo that was the site of Scipio's victories over Hasdrubal (209 B.C.), and over Mago and Masinissa (206 B.C.)
A settlement of Samnium, within the territory of the Hirpini, that lay close to the frontiers of Apulia. The site is described only by Horace in his famous trip to Brundisium.
A settlement of Tarraconensis located at the confluence of the Ter and the Onyar rivers, Gerunda was the chief town of the Gerundenses. Modern Girona in Spain.
A settlement of ancient Egypt, modern Kasr el-Saijad.

A settlement of northwestern Sardinia, located at the mouth of the Mannu River. The site served as a port in Phoenician, Carthaginian, and Roman phases of occupation. The modern Porto Torres stands on the site, about 10 miles distant from Sassari.
A settlement of the Allobroges in Gallia Narbonensis that became a Roman colony in 47 BC.
A settlement of the Caletes in Gallia Belgica
A settlement of the Edones, conquered by the Persians and given to Histiaios of Miletos in 513 BC, then briefly colonised by Milesians after the Ionian Revolt. It was conquered by Macedon in 356 BC.
A settlement of the Oenotrians and the Lucani dating to the seventh through third centuries B.C. Its ancient name is unknown.
A settlement of the Segovellauni in Gallia Narbonensis.
A settlement of the Sicani on the northern coast of Sicily, conquered by the Athenians in 415 BC.
A settlement of the Treveri (ancient name unknown) at modern Mamer in Luxembourg.
A settlement of the indigenous Messapii that was refounded under Roman influence in the third century B.C.
A settlement on Pontia Ins. The largest of the Pontine Islands, Pontia lies 33 km south of Cape Circeo on the Italian mainland.
A settlement on the coast of south-western Corsica, in the territory of the Titianoi.
A settlement on the island of Rhodes.
A settlement on the island of Salamis that was sieged by Cnemus in 429 BC.
A settlement south of Ankara that served as the seat of Castor the Elder, the tetrarch of the Tectosages.
A seventh- and eighth-century BC Punic sanctuary on the Awali river dedicated to Eshmun, the Phoenician god of healing.
A signal tower situated on Hadrian's Wall.
A significant Hellenistic city that served as a capital of both the Seleucid and Parthian empires. The city was founded by Seleucus Nicator.
A significant Hellenistic settlement of Pisidia that received an Augustan colony, taking the name Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Cremnensium.
A significant pre-Roman and Roman site that became a Roman municipium.
A significant site, estimated at 150 hectares during the Sassanian period, contracting to 100 hectares during the Early Islamic-Sāmarrān period.
A site first mentioned (A.D. 6) as a winter camp of Tiberius, Carnuntum eventually became a legionary base and the seat of the governor for Pannonia.
A site in Cilicia Aspera near Demirtaş.
A site in Roman Britain located some 20 km northwest of Gloucester along the road leading towards the Wye valley. Numismatic evidence suggests possible Roman military presence.
A site in the Loire estuary that served as a port.
A site located along the Roman frontier (limes) in Germania Inferior.
A site located near the bottom of the Great Syrtis which marked the boundary between the territories of Carthage and Cyrene, and later between Tripolitana and Cyrenaica.
A site that originated as a Roman castrum and developed into a town from the fifth century onward. Archaeological remains date from the Roman, Byzantine, and Early Muslim periods.

A site to the west of modern Praeneste in Italy where surface material, remains of structures, and graves were discovered in the 19th century. These finds provide evidence for a settlement possibly dating to as early as the fifth or fourth century BCE but with likely occupation throughout the subsequent Roman period.

A site with Phoenician origins (founded ca. 730-700 B.C.) located in southwestern Sardinia. Site of a Roman naval victory against Carthage by Gaius Sulpicius Paterculus in 258 B.C. during the First Punic War.

A site with a long history of occupation, beginning in the Mesolithic period. In the Roman imperial period, a Roman auxiliary fort replaces a La Tène phase of occupation. A vicus is associated with the fort.
A site with settlement origins in the Bronze and Iron Ages, Rhegion was eventually colonized by Chalcis in either 743 or 730 BCE.
A sixth century BC colony of Miletus founded on the Gulf of Taman.
A sixth century BC settlement on the Nile in Lower Nubia.
A small Hellenistic town excavated on the Trypitos promontory E of Siteia, Lasithi Crete. It is probably to be identified with Polichna, attested in ancient literary sources.
A small Roman fort.
A small Roman settlement near Ermine Street and Stane Street was established in the second half of the first century CE at Braughing, United Kingdom.
A small Roman-era settlement noted by Gsell in AAA, whence BAtlas 30 inset 2
A small city of northern Italy with Roman origins.

A small island in the Stagnone Lagoon of western Sicily, Motya has evidence for quite ancient settlement, including a significant Punic phase. The settlement on the island was destroyed by Syracuse in 379 BC. At one point, the island was connected to the mainland via a causeway.

A small oasis lying about 60 km north west of Kharga, on the escarpment outlining the depression. It was the only water source along the Darb Ain Amur, one of the two tracks that linked Kharga and Dakhla. The archaeological remains consist of a Late Period stone temple and a large cemetery. Surveyed between 2006 and 2011 by the North Kharga Oasis Survey project.
A small site in Latium (?1.2 hectares) that may have been fortified as early as the eighth century BCE.
A small, fortified hilltop with evidence of nearby Sikel tombs. The Greek fortifications have been speculatively attributed to Hippokrates of Gela (ca. 495 B.C.).

A small, rectangular fortress on a raised terrace of land, located near the, possibly earlier, Xylokastro fortification on Mt. Plakoto in the modern municipal unit of Palairos, Aetolia-Acarnania Regional Unit, Greece.
A square, stone tower known today as Varnava Tower (Ο πύργος του Βαρνάβα), located outside the modern village of Varnava in Greece.
A statio on the road from Nuceria to Ancona.
A station located along the course of the Danube River in Lower Pannonia between Acumincum (Stari Slankamen) and Malata-Bononia.
A station on the Via Cassia attested in an inscription dated to A.D. 379-383.

A strategic Volscian city that had come under Roman control by 509 B.C.; a Roman citizen colony was established there in 329 B.C. The site is particularly notable for the remains of the terraced sanctuary of Iuppiter Anxur.

A tell known today as "Yumuktepe" is located at modern Mersin in Turkey. Excavations there, beginning in the 20th century, have provided evidence for continuous and/or successive human settlement beginning in the Neolithic period. Scholars believe that the names "Ingirâ" (found in Akkadian sources) and "Anchiale(ia)" (found in Greco-Roman sources) are to be associated with the site.

A tell settlement, known today as Tehouda, located in modern Algeria and mentioned by Pliny the Elder. Archaeological remains at the site provide evidence for mud-brick fortification walls and might be consistent with a sixth century reoccupation and Byzantine garrison of a "Dabousis" recorded by Procopius.
A tell settlement, located 20km west of Thessaloniki.
A temporary Roman camp of Flavian date.
A temporary Roman marching camp.
A third-century A.D. Roman fort that was part of the Saxon Shore fortification system.
A tower situated on Hadrian's Wall.
A town founded as Vicus Novanensis, later named simply Ad Novas, along the Via Appia.

A town in Achaia Phthiotis, which usually provided one of the regions' two representatives to the Delphic Amphiktyony. It became part of the Aetolian League around 260 BC and part of the Thessalian League in 189 BC. It remained inhabited through the Roman Imperial period and into Byzantine times. The modern town of Avaritsa is nearby.
A town in Lucania that was the location of a military engagement between Hannibal and Marcus Claudius Marcellus in 210 B.C.
A town in ancient Apulia located between Larinum and Sipontum. Rome took control of the site in 318 BC, granting it municipal status.
A town in the Hestiaiotis region between Metropolis and Gomphoi. Now modern Phanari, where the visible architecture on the acropolis largely belongs to Byzantine and Ottoman fortresses.
A town known from Ptolemy, Makopsisa (modern Macomer) is located in the Nuoro province of Sardinia.

A town of Caria located 25 km east of Miletos on the Ionian coast, Heraclea was located on the lower slopes of Mt. Latmos. Once a part of the Delian League, the city fell to Mausolos in the fourth century B.C. and his philhellene policy accounts for its change of name.
A town of Liguria located near the source of the Po River (ancient Padus).
A town of Lycia located on the southern slope of Mt. Cragus and northwest of the mouth of the Xanthus river.
A town of Mauretania Tingitana and a Roman colony.
A town of Mygdonia in Macedonia, located near the river carrying the waters of the lake Bolbe to the Strymonic gulf.
A town of Triphylia in ancient Elis.
A town of ancient Latium along the line of the Via Appia, Bovillae is traditionally considered to be a colony of Alba Longa and was one of the thirty cities of the Latin League.
A town of southwest Gaul founded ca. 20 BC, Mediolanum Santonum was connected with the Roman road network that served Burdigala.

A town of the Aequi along the Marsic frontier where the Romans established a Latin colony in 304/3 B.C. Alba Fucens was a significant center of the middle republican period and became a place where Rome kept state prisoners, including Syphax of Numidia, Perseus of Macedonia, and Bituitus, king of the Arverni.
A town of the Elymians located between Lilybaeum and Entella.
A town of the Marsi in the valley of the Liris River.
A town of the Ozolian Locrians, situated at the western entrance of the Crissaean Gulf.
A town of the Peucetii in Apulia.
A town of the Peucetii in South Italy, Norba was conquered by the Romans in 268 BCE and was abandoned in the fifth century CE.
A town of the Sabines mentioned by Pliny the Elder.
A town on the Via Aemilia that was the site of a battle waged between M. Antonius and Hirtius and Pansa during the siege of Mutina.
A town that was part of the tetrapolis of Doris in ancient Greece.

A vicus of the Vestini located in the upper Aterno valley in Abruzzo. The ancient settlement was located some 15 km south of modern L'Aquila, in the vicinity of S. Maria di Forfona near Barisciano. Furfo lay on the Via Claudia Nova between Amiternum and Peltuinum.
A vicus of the civitas Menapiorum.
A vicus of the civitas Nerviorum.

A villa of Roman Imperial date, attributed to Herodes Atticus and his heirs. The modern name comes from the nearby Moni Loukous, or monastery of Loukou (St. Luke?), which may sit above an early Christian church.
A village of the Marrucini, forming a station on the Via Claudia Valeria between Corfinium and Teate.

AAA recorded a prehistoric site in a ravine and a separate Roman site on a height, both south of this spring. BAtlas placed a settlement symbol for the Roman site roughly coincident with what is now the modern town of Sidi Lakhdar in Algeria's Mostaganem province.

Abai was an ancient town in Phocis, said to have been founded by the Argive Abas. It has been identified with a hilltop, fortified archaeological site known as Palaiokhori, near modern Exarchos. The site of an oracular sanctuary of Apollo and Artemis associated with Abai in ancient literature has been identified at nearby Kallipodi.
Abdera was a coastal city located on Cape Bulustra, near the estuary of the river Nestos.
Abella was an ancient settlement of Campania of Samnite origin.
Abellinum was a settlement of the Hirpini in Campania.
Abila was a Ptolemaic town located in northern Palestine. Antiochus III conquered it and Pompeius Magnus later freed it in 64 B.C. Becoming autonomous thereafter, Abila became part of the Decapolis.
Abrittus was the site of a Roman fortress and settlement, located near modern Razgrad, Bulgaria.

Abundant spolia, artifacts, and building foundations provide evidence for an ancient settlement in the area of modern Kastro ano Diakopto and the church of Ag. Athanasios on the hill above it to the west. It is probably to be identified with ancient Boura, an attested settlement of Achaia.
Abusina was the site of a Roman auxiliary fort along the Danube, some 30 km SW of Regensburg (at the modern village of Eining).

According to Apollodorus, Archelaos relocated the population of coastal ancient Pydna (q.v.), remains of which lie on the southern edge of modern Marygialos, to a new, inland site. Scholars believe that, by the Roman era, this site had become or moved to the area of modern Kitros, although no definitive urban center has yet been identified. Several locations between Marygialos, Kitros, and Alonia (further inland and north of Kitros) have produced related funerary material and epigraphy.
According to Pliny, Nagia was the largest center of the Gebanitae in southern Arabia.

According to Polybius, this ancient settlement of Aetolia was razed by Philip of Macedon. Stephanus of Byzantium places Metapa in Acarnania. Pritchett (SAGT) meticulously describes the vicinity and identifies the site of Metapa based on ancient stone blocks in conditions of reuse and abandonment, as well as plentiful ceramic sherds in the vicinity of an older and modern church of the Analipsis on the lake shore just east of the modern village of Daphnias.
According to Strabo, Parapotamioi "is a settlement on the Cephissus River near Phanoteus and Chaeroneia and Elateia".
According to the Antonine Itinerary, ‘Vernemeto’ was located 13 Roman miles north of Ratae Coritanorum (Leicester) along the Fosse Way.
According to the Historic England registry, a Roman signal station/fortlet was identified at Goldsborough. This station was part of a system along the cliffs of north-east Yorkshire.
Acelum (modern Asolo) was an ancient settlement of the Veneti.
Acerrae was an ancient Oscan city of Campania, perhaps originally named Akeru. The Romans granted it civitas sine suffragio in 332 BC.
Acharnai (N) was the largest deme of ancient Attika, the sole inland deme of the tribe Oineis.
Acidava was the site of a Roman castrum in Dacia.
Acquarossa was an Etruscan settlement that was abandoned in the sixth century BC. The settlement occupied a steep-sided plateau and had an area of approximately 32 ha. Its ancient name is unknown.

Acumincum (modern Stari Slankamen in Serbia) was a settlement of the Scordisci that was later conquered by the Romans. During the Flavian period, the Cohors I Britannica equitata and II Adjutrix were based there.
Adranon was a settlement founded ca. 400 B.C. on the western slopes of mount Aetna.
Aefula was an ancient settlement of Latium that had disappeared by the time of Pliny the Elder, although the cult of Bona Dea there continued to flourish.
Aegida was an ancient town of Histria that is mentioned only by Pliny the Elder.
Aequiculi was a municipium in the territory of the Aequi.
Aequinoctium was the site of a Roman fort on the Danube in Upper Pannonia.

Aequum Tuticum/Equus Tuticus was an ancient Oscan town. The settlement was located near the intersection of the Via Traiana and the Via Herculia in the territory of the Hirpini. The site is now in the territory of the modern Italian town of Ariano Irpino.
After the sacking of Jerusalem, Vespasian settled Roman veterans on a new town site located between Mt. Gerizim and Mt. Ebal. The new Roman colony was built on the site of Mabartha.
Agatha (modern Agde), also known as Agatha Tyche, was a colonial foundation of ca. 525 B.C. The colony was founded by Phocaean Greeks from Massilia.
Aginnum (modern Agen) was the capital of the Nitiobriges in Gaul.

Agrai was a district of ancient Athens located south of the Ilissos River. Pausanias describes the temple of Artemis Agrotera as being located there. It was also the site of the Lesser Mysteries of Eleusis.
Aguntum was an ancient settlement of Noricum that received municipal status under Claudius.
Aianteion was a port town in the Troad located near the putative Tomb of Ajax, with which it shared a name.
Aigai(ai)/Aegeae (modern Yumurtalık, Turkey) is an ancient city in Cilicia.
Aigosthena was a fortified city of in the Megaris that served as one of Megara's ports. In the Hellenistic period, it became an autonomous city.
Ain Dara, located northwest of Aleppo, Syria, is noted for the remains of an Iron Age Syro-Hittite temple.
Ain Ouassel or Ain Wassel is a rural archaeological site dated to the early Byzantine period. The site contained a mix-use farm.

Aithalidai/Hybadai? was a deme of ancient Attica. Following the Cleisthenic reforms, Aethalidae was assigned to the phyle of Leontis. After 307/6 BCE, it belonged to the phyle of Antigonis. The deme's location is uncertain.
Aixone was an ancient coastal deme of the phyle Kekropis, located on the west coast of Attica south of Athens in the area of modern Glyphada.
Aizanoi was an ancient Roman city located in western Anatolia.
Akragas/Agrigentum was an ancient city of Sicily and is now known as Agrigento. The Archaeological Area of Agrigento was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997.
Akrai, an ancient city of Sicily, originated as a colony founded by Syracuse in 664 B.C., making it the first of the city's three colonial foundations.

Akriai or Acriae was a settlement of ancient Laconia, located to the south of the modern Greek village of Kokkinia (municipality of Evrotas). According to Strabo, the Eurotas river flows into the sea between Akriai and Gythium.

Akrotiri is the modern name of an archaeological site located on the island of Thera (modern Santorini) where a Minoan Bronze Age settlement flourished before being destroyed by a volcanic eruption ca. 1627 B.C. The site has been under scientific excavation since 1967.
Alabanda/Antiocheia Chrysaoron was an ancient city of Caria.
Alabum was a Roman fort in Britain that was occupied until the fourth century A.D.

Alb(i)um Intimilium/Albintimilium (modern Ventimiglia) was the main settlement of the Ligurian tribe of the Intemelii. In the 2nd century BC, it came under the control of the Roman Republic. Albintimilium became a municipium in 89 BC in the tribus Falerna. In the same period, the city walls were built, with several towers. The city flourished in the early Imperial period, with baths, an aqueduct, and a theater. In the 6th and early 7th century, it was a Byzantine kastron, coming under the control of the Longobards in 641. During the 7th and 8th centuries, the Roman city was slowly abandoned in favour of a smaller hilltop settlement focused around the Cathedral.
Alba Helviorum was the capital of the Helvii in Gallia Narbonensis.

Alba Longa, located in the Alban Hills southeast of Rome, was the chief city and founder of the Latin League. Conflict with Rome caused Alba's destruction in the seventh century B.C. The legendary history of Romulus and Remus connects them to the royal lineage of the city. The ancient city is probably to be located at and around the site of modern Castel Gandolfo.
Alba Pompeia (modern Alba) was a Celtic and Ligurian settlement that entered into the Roman sphere during the late Republican period. In Imperial times, Alba was the birthplace of Pertinax.
Albaniana was the site of a castellum that was part of the Roman frontier system (limes) of Germania Inferior.

Alchester was the site of a fortified Roman town located 17 kilometers to the northeast of Oxford. The site was of Claudian date and likely on the site of a Pre-Roman Iron Age settlement. It may have been one of the earliest legionary bases in Britannia.
Alebaece Reiorum Apollinarium/Apollinaris Reiorum/Reii was the capital of the tribe of the Reii. Modern Riez in France's Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department.

Almus (now Lom, Bulgaria) was a place in Moesia Inferior located on the southern bank of the Danube River and near the mouth of a river of the same name (Almus). Both places are noted on the Tabula Peutingeriana.
Alopeke was the only city deme of the tribe Antiochis in Attica
Alsium served as a port for Caere, together with Fregenae. A Roman colony was established ca. 245 BCE. The Antonine Itinerary places it 18 Roman miles from Portus at the mouth of the Tiber.

Also known as Burwen Castle, this site in North Yorkshire has produced evidence for a succession of two superimposed Roman forts. One or both of them are probably to be identified with the name Olenacum, preserved in ancient sources.
Also known as Germanicopolis or Germanopolis. An ancient settlement in Paphlagonia, modern Çankırı in Turkey.
Althiburos was a city of Africa Proconsularis that became a municipium under Hadrian and a colonia during the third century A.D.

Although the Classical/Hellenistic city was deserted in Pausanias' day, archaeology reveals that the area of modern Nafplio and its natural harbor on the Argolic Gulf was repeatedly a site of habitation and human activity from the Neolithic period to the modern day. Remains of a Hellenistic acropolis wall have been identified under the later Byzantine (with subsequent accretions and modifications) fort.
Altinum was the capital of the Veneti of northern Italy. The site was destroyed by Attila in 452 CE.
Amaseia (modern Amasya) was a naturally fortified settlement in the Pontic mountains near the Black Sea. It served as the capital of the kingdom of Pontus from ca. 300 BC to 183 BC.
Amathous, an ancient royal city of Cyprus.

Ambracia (modern Arta) was an ancient city of central Greece, founded as a colony of Corinth in the seventh century BCE. It was located near the Ambracian Gulf along the course of the river Arachthos.
Ameria, claimed by Cato the Elder (quoted by Pliny) as the oldest town in Umbria, was an important center that may have gained Roman municipal status as early as 338 B.C., following the Latin War.

Amiternum was an ancient settlement of the Sabines that Rome captured in 293 BC. The settlement was situated at the intersection of four Roman roads: the Via Caecilia, the Via Claudia Nova, and the two branches of the Via Salaria. The historian Sallust was born at Amiternum in 86 B.C.
Amyklai was an ancient settlement located near Sparta in the plain by the Eurotas river to the east of the Taygetus mountains.
An 8-hectare Romano-British settlement that developed in the 60s AD and continued in use until the fourth century.
An Achaean colony in Magna Graecia established in 710 BC by the oikist Myscellus from the city of Rhypes in the Peloponnese.
An Arabian city of lower Mesopotamia, located some 420 km south-east of Baghdad.

An Aramaean principality and Neo-Assyrian provincial capital founded on the site of an extinct Neolithic settlement. Settled through Hellenistic times, it was abandoned at the end of the first century BCE.
