Remains of a Roman-era site in the modern Algerian municipal territory of el Karimia (Chlef province).

Remains of a presumably Roman settlement were identified but not excavated in the 20th century at the "seyyid" or "marabout" of "Sidi Larbi Boujema", which is said to be situated on the west side of the river Sabou, along what is now the Route Nationale 27 about 5 kilometers south of modern Mechra bel Ksiri in Morocco's Sefsaf commune (Sidi Kacem Province). This location corresponds to the "Al-Arabi Bou Jemaa" cemetery recorded in Google Maps (2025) and visible in satellite imagery. Euzennat (repeating the same in PECS and BAtlDir) tenatively identified the ruins here with (Vo)pisciana (q.v.), which is attested in the Antonine itinerary, but more recent scholarship has followed Rebuffat 2000 in preferring Souq el Arbaâ du Gharb (see "Souk el Arba").
Remains of a ruined village with mud brick structures, qanat, and an associated necropolis of Roman date all located 3-5 km west of ancient Dush (Egypt).
Remains of an ancient coastal settlement located between modern Al-Raafah and Al Ramlah in the United Arab Emirates. It is possibly to be identified with ancient Omana, mentioned in Roman sources.

Remains of an ancient fortification recorded by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas). The location should lie within a kilometer of the BAtlas coordinates: a point east-northeast of modern Bousâada in the municipal territory of modern At Muḥli/Beni Mouhli in Algeria's Setif province.

Remains of an ancient settlement of Roman date, recorded by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas). The location should lie within a kilometer of the BAtlas coordinates: a point near modern Bir el Kerma, which is located in the modern municipal territory of Tixter (Bordj Bou Arreridj willaya).

Remains of an ancient village in the Golan that produced Greek and Hebrew Inscriptions probably associated with a synagogue. The site is described by Urman et al. as occupying "two low hills near a group of springs about two kilometers northeast of Qaṣrin."
Remains of fortifications dating to the Late Roman period.

Remnants of an ancient settlement have been identified south and east of the modern beach village of Nopigeia on Crete that date to at least the 5th century BCE. The church of Agios Georgios Nopigion, which is located between Nopigia and Drapania, was built on the remains of a Roman-era bath complex. A single, late source (Aelian) provides the name Mithymna, which may have belonged to this settlement. Bronze Age remains have also been identified in the vicinity.
Rhaga(i), now the city of Rey in Iran, was an important settlement of the Medes that declined after the Mongol invasions.
Rhamnous was an ancient settlement of Attica adjacent to the Euboean Strait and a coastal deme of the tribe Aiantis.
Rigomagus (Remagen) was the site of a Roman fort built west of the Rhine.

Robert argued for reading "ἔμβολος" in a fragmentary funerary epigram found in the area of Beyköy, Turkey, as a toponym. He argues, with reference to early travelers' accounts of antiquities in the area, for a nearby location for this putative settlement, probably up the gorge of the Ugursuyu.
Roccagloriosa was a fortified Lucanian settlement of the fourth and third centuries BCE.

Roman Lagentium (modern Castleford) is the site of a series of forts, beginning with a Flavian fort that was later replaced by a second-century fort. The site of the fort was occupied from ca. A.D. 80 to 150 while the vicus remained occupied until the fourth century.
Roman London was established ca. A.D. 43.
Roman city situated on mineral springs known today as Terme di Cotilia or Terme di Vespasiano in the Sabina region, Italy
Roman fort and civil settlement or castrum established by the Roman legions invading Wales and now located at Abergavenny.
Roman fort and fortlet on the Antonine Wall, Scotland.
Roman fort and vicus in Netherby.
Roman fort at present day Lancaster.
Roman fort at present-day Beckfoot. Part of the Cumbrian coastal defenses.

Roman fort at the mouth of the modern Chorokhi river in Colchis, established in 63 or 64 CE, rebuilt under Trajan and Hadrian, when it was garrisoned with cohorts from the legio V Macedonica. It was destroyed by an earthquake c. 140 CE, rebuilt, and finally abandoned around 257 CE. Extensive excavations have been undertaken since 2014.
Roman fort built during Agricola's campaign in Scotland.
Roman fort in Brough, England.
Roman fort in Cardean, Scotland.
Roman fort in Germany.
Roman fort in Noricum
Roman fort in present day Usk
Roman fort near Bowes.
Roman fort near present-day Carrawburgh.
Roman fort of mid-first century date and possible later vicus associated near Monmouth, UK
Roman fort of the Saxon Shore
Roman fort on Hadrian's wall in Stanwix.
Roman fort on the Antonine Wall, in East Dunbartonshire, Scotland
Roman fort overlooking the Clyde Estuary, Scotland.
Roman fort situated on the Antonine Wall.
Roman fort, cited: BAtlas 9 D6 Aballava
Roman fortlet and fort on the Antonine Wall in West Dunbartonshire, Scotland.
Roman fortlet then settlement near Stoke by Newark, United Kingdom
Roman legionary fortress at present-day Caerleon. Base of Legio II Augusta from ca. A.D. 75-300. Also known as Isca Augusta and Isca Silurum.
Roman ruins noted by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas) in the area of modern Souk el Khemis in Algeria's Bouira province.
Roman town at present day Rochester, cited: BAtlas 8 H3 Durobrivae
Roman town in present-day Lincolnshire. Candidate location for Bannovallum (the other being Horncastle).
Roman/late antique settlement, with substantial remains of an industrial area, a church complex, and a mud-brick temple reused as a ceramic workshop.
Roman/late antique settlement, with visible remains of streets and mud-brick structures, including a church, two pigeon towers, and possibly residential units. Largely unexcavated.
Romano-British settlement and military complex located at present day Water Eaton, UK
Romano-British settlement of Easton Grey in Wiltshire, situated on the Foss Way. Referred to in some earlier sources as 'White Walls'.
Rubi was a statio in Apulia, located along the Via Minucia.
Ruins of a Roman era settlement noted by Gsell (AAA, whence BAtlas) at Koudiat el Azari, on a slope to the north above the Oued Kassob.

Ruins of an ancient town located in a now-uninhabited forest area near the modern Turkish town of Kapaklı in the Demre district of Antalya province. Its ancient name is known only from fragmentary epigraphic sources of the Hellenistic period, but archaeological investigation has demonstrated occupation and development from the 3rd century BCE through late antiquity, with some modest habitation continuing in the medieval period.

Ruins of an old town or castle on the tall "Felsberg Egri Kalch" near the mouth of the Halys river that were formerly posited as an identification for Herodotus' "Pteria" (thus RE whence BAtlas 87, which labeled Eğrikale with "Pteria" using a hollow settlement symbol). Pteria is now thought much more probably to be associated with the large 7th/6th century site at Kerkenes Dağı to the southwest, q.v.

Ruins of the walled acropolis of ancient Isinda in Lycia are variously said by modern scholars to be located either "above" or 2-3km south of the modern Turkish village of Belenli, which is in Antalya province. BAtlas and OpenStreetMap generally agree (within their accuracy and precision limits) with the location further south.
Rusicade/Thapsus was the port of Cirta and a Roman colonia, located at the mouth of the small river Thapsus.

S. Vincenzo al Volturno is a multi-period settlement. In pre-Roman times, a phase of Samnite occupation has been identified. By the fifth century A.D., the site was occupied by a large agricultural estate (villa) that was abandoned in the later fifth century, only to be replaced by a Christian church.
Saalburg was a Roman auxiliary castrum associated with the Limes Germanicus.
Sabucina was a major indigenous center in central Sicily that was wealthiest in the sixth and fifth centuries BC; it may have been connected with sulfur mining.
Sacer Mons is a hill on the banks of the Anio River and is connected, traditionally, with the episode of the secession of the Roman plebs of 494 BC.

Sacriportus is an ancient site of Latium located between Signia and Praeneste, although its precise location is no longer known. It was the site of a decisive battle between Caius Marius and Lucius Cornelius Sulla.
Saena was an Etruscan city that received a Roman colony (Saena Iulia) in the time of Augustus.
Saetabis was a town of the Contestani in Hispania Tarraconensis. It has been identified with the modern Spanish town of Xàtiva in the province of Valencia.
Sagalassos is an ancient city in Pisidia that was later part of the Roman province of Galatia. The city flourished until natural disasters and disease led to its decline in the sixth century AD.

Sais was an ancient Egyptian town located in the Western Nile Delta on the Canopic branch of the Nile River. It served as the provincial capital of Sap-Meh, the fifth nome of Lower Egypt, and became a capital during the Twenty-fourth Dynasty (ca. 732–720 BC) as well as during the Late Period. Herodotus claimed that Osiris was buried at Sais. Other Greek authors, including Plato, maintained a connection between Sais and the goddess Athena.
Sal(a)pia(i)/Salinae was an ancient city of Daunia.

Salinae is a Romano-British site of ca. 20 ha located at the confluence of the Dane and Croco rivers, some 30 km east of Chester. The site was occupied by the late first century A.D. and remained in use until the fourth century. The Roman road from Lancaster to Littlechester formed the main north-south street axis of the site.
Salmantica (modern Salamanca) was an indigenous Celtic center before falling to the Carthaginians and, later, the Romans.
Samaria/Sebaste was an ancient city of Iudaea. In 30 B.C., it passed under the control of Herod the Great and was renamed Sebaste in honor of the emperor Augustus.
Sanisera was a Roman settlement of Menorca.

Sardis was the capital of the Lydian Empire, located in western Turkey. In 188 B.C. Sardis became a part of the Attalid kingdom, and thus it passed with the territory of Attalus III to Rome in 133 B.C.
Sarsina was a town of the Umbri that was captured by Cornelius Scipio in 271 B.C. and was the birthplace of the Latin author Plautus. The necropolis at Sarsina has been extensively studied.
Sarteano is located between the Val d'Orcia and the Valdichiana. It is known in particular for its rich evidence of Etruscan funerary culture.
Satala was the station of the Legio XV Apollinaris.
Saticula was a Samnite site in Campania that received a Latin colony in 313 B.C.
Savo/Vicus Virginis? (modern Savona) was a Ligurian settlement that came under Roman influence after the Second Punic War.

Scamnum is a road station located in Messapia that is mentioned on the Tabula Peutingeriana. It is perhaps to be identified with excavations at the site of Muro Tenente that have revealed long term occupation levels, beginning from the Neolithic period.
Scarponna was a station along the road from Langres to Trier, located at a crossing on the Moselle River.

Scholars associated the ancient place Forentum with Lavello in south Italy. In antiquity, this was an indigenous center active from the Early Iron Age that gradually manifested the material culture of Greek colonists in Magna Graecia.
Scicli is the site of settlement beginning in the third millennium BC. The town of Scicli is believed to have been founded by Sicels ca. 300 BC.
Scupi (modern Skopje, Macedonia (Macedonian: Скопје)) has been the site of human settlement since ca. 4000 BC.
Scylletium/Scolacium was an ancient settlement in Bruttium located on the Gulf of Squillace.
Sebennytos was an ancient city of Lower Egypt located on the Sebennytic branch of the Nile River. It was the capital of Lower Egypt's twelfth nome (the Sebennyte nome).

Second site of the ancient Greek city of Pleuron, built after the destruction of the original location in the 3rd century BCE. This second site boasts significant excavated remains and is located on the southern slope of Mount Aracynthus near modern Kato Retsina.
See https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/540921/
See: https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/580093
Segedunum was a Roman fort located at modern-day Wallsend, North Tyneside in the northeast of England. The fort was located at the eastern end of Hadrian's Wall.
Segelocum was a settlement of Roman Britain located along the road from Lincoln to Doncaster where it crossed the river Trent.
Segestica/Siscia is an Iron Age settlement recorded by Strabo. It was located at the confluence of three rivers and was used as a staging area for a campaign against the Dacians.
Segida Augurina (Palma del Río)
Segisamo was located on the road from Tarraco to Asturica.
Segobriga was an Ibero-Roman city.
Segodunum was a Gallic oppidum and later a Gallo-Roman town. It has been identified by scholars with modern Rodez.
Segovia, originally of Celtiberian origin, became a Roman settlement. It is perhaps the site where Metellus defeated Hirtuleius, the general of Sertorius, in 75 B.C.
Seleucia Sidera was an ancient city in the northern part of Pisidia, Anatolia, founded by Seleucus I Nicator or Antiochus I Soter in order to protect the military road across northern Pisidia.
Seleucia/Sliq Kharawta was a city founded on the Tigris River by Seleukos I Nikator.
Seleucid kings (either Seleucus I Nicator or Antiochus I Soter), likely founded Cyrrhus in the first half of the third century B.C.
Selge was an important city of Pisidia; Strabo claims it was founded as a Spartan colony.

Selinous/Traianopolis was a city of Cilicia Aspera and counted among the chief coastal cities of Cilicia. It is perhaps best known as the place where Trajan died in A.D. 117 en route to Rome from his campaigns in the East.

Senonian Gauls founded Sena Gallica at the mouth of the Misa River in the fourth century B.C. This place became the site of Rome's earliest colony on the Adriatic seaboard before 280 B.C. Pompeius Magnus destroyed the city in 82 B.C.
Septempeda was an ancient settlement of Picenum. Its Roman phase began as a conciliabulum in the third century B.C.
Sestinum was an ancient place in Umbria near the headwaters of the river Pisaurus. Pliny mentions the site, and its ancient name is preserved in modern toponymy.
Setelsis was a settlement of the Jaccetani in Hispania Tarraconensis.

Settlement associated with Punic and Roman quarries known today as Ghar El Kebir (previously and perhaps in error: Rhar-el-Kebir). The complex is perhaps to be associated with the ancient name Latomiai.

Settlement in central Georgia showing signs of continuous inhabitation from the third millennium BCE through the present. It was a substantial center of the region in the 4th century BCE and in the early Medieval period (6th-7th centuries CE).
Settlement located in the modern town of Eceabat on the Gallipoli Peninsula containing signs of continuous habitation from the 3rd millennium BCE through the Medieval period.
Settlement on the Aegean island of Naxos.
Settlement on the island of Capreae.
Settlement/fortress descibed by Stählin (1924, 224-225); Béquignon (1937, 322-324; Fig. 16).

Seuthopolis was an ancient Thracian city that followed Hellenistic paradigms in terms of city planning. The city was founded by the Thracian king Seuthes III in the late fourth century BC and served as the capital of the Odrysian kingdom. Located near the modern city of Казанлъ̀к (Kazanlak) in Bulgaria, the site was excavated in the 1940s and subsequently submerged by the filling of the Koprinka reservoir.
Sexi/Saxetanum (modern Almuñécar) was a Phoenician colony established ca. 800 BC that eventually became a Roman one (Sexi Firmum Iulium).
Sextantio was a Celtic settlement at a ford on the Ledus fl. and later became a Gallo-Roman town.
Shepton Mallet is located along the Fosse Way, midway between the Roman towns of Bath and Ilchester.
Sicca Veneria was an important Punic and Roman city located in what is now Tunisia.

Sicyon/Demetrias was an important ancient city of the Corinthiad, located some 26 km to the west of Corinth. The city had a long history, beginning in the Archaic period when Orthagorid tyrants ruled it. It flourished in later Archaic and Classical times, was a member of the Peloponnesian League, and became a center of Theban power after 371 B.C. The city was long noted for its association with fine arts and during the fourth century B.C. produced the famous sculptor Lysippos. Under Aratos, Sicyon joined the Achaean League in 251 B.C. By the time Pausanias visited the site, declining political fortunes and disastrous earthquakes had reduced it to a ruinous state.
Sidon/Col. Aurelia Pia is an ancient maritime city and Phoenician metropolis
Sigeion was located in the northwest part of the Troad at the mouth of the Scamander River.
Sillyon was an ancient Graeco-Pamphylian fortress and city near Attaleia in Pamphylia, on the southern coast Asia Minor.
Silvium (modern Gravina in Puglia) was founded as a Greek colony. It was a town on the frontier of the Peucetii.
Singilia Barba was the site of a Roman municipium near Antequera, Málaga, Spain.
Sinope (modern Sinop, Turkey) on the Black Sea has been a major port since the time of the Hittites.

Sipous/Sipontum was a Greek colony that fell first under Samnite control, then was later taken by Alexander of Epirus. The site became a Roman colony in 189 BC. Legend ascribed its foundation to the hero Diomedes.

Sippar (or Zimbir) was an ancient city located on the east bank of the Euphrates river at the site of modern Tell Abu Habbah. In order to avoid confusing this site with its sister city of Sippar-Amnanum (Tell ed-Der), it is sometimes labeled as Sippar-Yahrurum.
Siris was an ancient Greek colonial city of Magna Graecia situated at the mouth of the Siris (modern Sinni) river. The city was founded by Ionian Greeks between 690 and 660 BC.

Site in the Shami Valley (Khuzestan Province, Iran), a settlement or sanctuary of the Parthian period (ca. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE). In 1936, a team led by Marc Aurel Stein uncovered a bronze sculpture (the "Shami statue") at the site.
Site of Roman fort occupied during the Antonine period, located 4.5 miles NNW of Castle Rock, Edinburgh.
Site of Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
Site of Roman forts and temporary camps in Dalginross, Scotland.
Site of Roman settlement attested in the Ravenna Cosmography, referring to either of the small towns situated at Caistor or Horncastle in Lincolnshire.
Site of Romano-British settlement or small town
Site of a Roman fort and civilian settlement in the Castlefield area of modern Manchester.
Site of a Roman fort occupied during the Flavian and Antonine periods. It lies 4 miles east of Jedburgh in the Scottish Borders, along the line of Dere Street.
Site of a Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
Site of a Roman fort that developed in a small Romano-British settlement
Site of a Roman fort that was first occupied ca. A.D. 55-65. The fort later moved to a new site during the governorship of Cn. Julius Agricola.
Site of a Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall.
Site of a Roman legionary fortress (ca. 67 A.D.) and later colonia (founded ca. 97-98 A.D.) at modern day Gloucester.
Site of a Roman settlement that is included on the Antonine Itinerary.
Site of a first-century A.D. Roman fort and later Roman town.
Site of a fortress on the eastern frontier of the Roman empire that was the setting for two famous sieges in 360.
Site of a late Bronze Age village in Calabria.
Site of a major Islamic capital that controlled the provinces of the Abbasid Empire extending from Tunisia to Central Asia for a century. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2007.
Site of a multi-phase Roman military encampment located in the modern town of Vitoria (Basque Country, Spain). Its ancient name is not known.
Site of a possible Roman Small Town.
Site of a small Roman fort between Castledykes and Tassiesholm. The fort was discovered in 1938 and excavated in 1961-66.
Site of a small Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
Site of a small Romano-British town.
Site of an Early Iron Age settlement on the western coast of the island of Andros (ninth-eighth centuries B.C.).
Site of an ancient settlement on the east coast of the Sea of Galilee (at modern Kursi) where port facilities, inscriptions, and a Byzantine monastery have been surveyed or excavated.

Site of an ancient settlement that flourished between the seventh century BCE and the early sixth century CE, located west across the Tiber from the modern village of Attigliano in Italy. Piammiano is probably to be identified with "Statonia", which is mentioned in ancient sources.
Site of an excavated amphora production facility in southern Thasos that may point to the existence of an associated settlement whose ancient name remains unknown.
Site of an important Bronze Age and Iron Age city located in the Bet She'an Valley about 5 km south of Beit She'an and 3 km west of the Jordan River.
Site of mid- to late-fourth century Roman fort.
Site, in modern France, of a Gallo-Roman settlement whose ancient name is not known.
Skidros or Scidrus was an ancient Greek city located on the Tyrrhenian coast of Lucania between Pyxus (Buxentum) and Laüs.
Skolopoeis was a settlement of Ionia. Herodotus notes the presence of a sanctuary sacred to the Eleusinian Demeter. The ancient place was located near Doğanbey in Asiatic Turkey.
Small Roman fort of Agricolan date in Scotland
Small Roman town on Ermine Street preceded by a fort and an extensive Iron Age settlement.

Sobata or Shivta is an ancient city in the Negev Desert located some 43 km southwest of Beersheba. The site was enrolled as a UNESCO World Heritage site, together with Haluza, Mamshit, and Avdat, in June 2005.
Soletum was a settlement in ancient Calabria.
Sorano was a Villanovan and, later, Etruscan settlement.

Sorrina was a small Etruscan settlement on Viterbo's Colle di San Lorenzo, of which some traces remain. Epigraphic evidence also attests to a Roman municipium - Surrina Nova - that was likely located between Viterbo and Lake Bullicame.

Sorviodunum (Old Sarum) is the site of pre-Roman habitation in Salisbury, England, where occupation began as early as 3,000 B.C. The oval Pre-Roman fort, covering some 11 ha, was re-used during the Roman and Norman periods.
Sorviodurum was the site of an auxiliary fort in Raetia (modern Straubing, Lower Bavaria).

South of modern Dar bel Amri, a settlement on the east side of the upper Beht river in Morocco, there are remnants of watch tower dating to the Roman imperial period. The fort's ancient name is not known.
Spalatum (modern Split, Croatia) is an ancient settlement on the Adriatic coast most noted for the palatial residence of the emperor Diocletian.
Sparta was a prominent city-state (polis) of ancient Greece.
Sphettos was an inland deme of Akamantis, in Attica, near modern Koropi.
St-Georges-du-Bois is the site of a Gallo-Roman amphitheater.
St-Peter-Port is a port city on the island of Guernsey.
Steiria was a deme of ancient Attica. It was located on the east coast of Attica, between Prasiae and Brauron, and belonged to the phyle of Pandionis.

Stonea, also referred to as Stonea Iron Age Camp, is located near March in the Cambridgeshire Fens in eastern England. Occupation of the hill fort begins ca. 500 BCE. Roman activity could be related to a military engagement in 47 CE mentioned by Tacitus. This engagement was between the Iceni tribe and Roman auxiliaries commanded by Ostorius Scapula.
Strageath is the site of a Roman camp located near the River Earn in eastern Scotland.
Stratos was the chief town of Acarnania. Modern Sourovigli in Greece.

Stryme was colonized by Greeks from the island of Thasos in the Archaic period, but by at least the 4th century BCE it appears to have fallen under the political and economic power of Maroneia. Stryme is probably to be identified with an archaeological site on the Molyvoti peninsula, where recent investigation by the Molyvoti, Thrace, Archaeological Project has demonstrated that the settlement was destroyed in the mid-fourth century and briefly reoccupied ca. 325 BCE before abandonment in the early 3rd century. In the Late Roman and Byzantine periods, there were small farmsteads on the peninsula and a settlement on the headland.
Stymphalos was a small but wealthy city of ancient Arcadia.

Styra was an ancient port city located in the southwestern part of Euboea that possessed also an inland acropolis (on the modern peak of Hagios Nikolaos), extensive quarries, and a series of large stone structures known today as drakospita (dragon's houses).
Suana (Sovana) has Etruscan origins but later became a Roman municipium. In the fifth century A.D. it became an episcopal see.
Suasa was the site of a Roman municipium in Umbria. It lies in the Piano Volpello along a road from Cales to Sena Gallica. Alaric razed the settlement in 409.
Suessula was an important ancient city of Campania.
Sufetula, the modern Sbeitla, was founded in the later first century A.D. and was located at a major road junction.
Sumelocenna was a Roman settlement on the Neckar River that served as the seat of the procurator of the saltus Sumelocennensis in the late first century AD.

Sybaris was an ancient city of Magna Graecia founded as an Achaean colony as early as 720 BCE on a plain that was drained by both the Crati and Sybaris rivers. Greeks from Kroton destroyed Sybaris ca. 510 BCE. Following this destruction, two successive cities, Thurii and Copia, respectively, were established on the same site. This topic is of particular interest to ancient authors, at least 70 of whom mention it.
Synnada, a Hellenistic and Roman crossroads town in Phrygia, present-day Şuhut, Turkey.
Tacape (modern Gabès) was a commercial city located on the Lesser Syrtis.
Tadinae (Sant'Antonio della Rasina to the west of Gualdo Tadino) is an ancient municipium of Umbria and was a road station on the Via Flaminia.
Tafis was the site of a Roman fortress in Nubia.
Takyris is an ancient royal Egyptian necropolis located in the desert on the west bank of the Nile.

Tamion? (modern Cardiff, Wales). A series of Roman forts occupied the same site in Cardiff, located on a river terrace adjacent to the River Taff, and represent continuous occupation from the late 50s AD until the late fourth century.
Tamuda was a city of Mauretania Tingitana. Pliny hints at a pre-Roman settlement that has been confirmed archaeologically.
Tanagra was an ancient settlement of Boeotia.
Tanais (located near modern Nedvigovska) was a city of the third century B.C. founded on the banks of the Tanais river by Bosporanian Greeks.
Taposiris Mikra was a town located to the east of Alexandria in the delta of the Nile river.
Tartessos was a harbor city and surrounding region located on the southern coast of the Iberian peninsula at the mouth of the Guadalquivir River.
Tarvisium (Treviso) is a settlement located in the plain of the Silis river, not far from the Via Claudia Augusta.
Tauromenium was an ancient city in Sicily founded in 358 B.C.
Tbilisi, the modern capital of Georgia, was the ancient Tiflīs and was founded in A.D. 455 or 458 when the capital of Georgia was transferred from Mtsk̲h̲eta.
Teanum Sidicinum (modern Teano) was the capital of the Oscan-speaking Sidicini tribe. The city likely submitted to Rome after 334 B.C.
Tegea was an ancient city of Arcadia. It is especially noted for its sanctuary dedicated to Athena Alea.
Teithras was an inland deme of Aigeis in Attica.
Tel Anafa is an archaeological site of the Upper Galilee in Israel. The site was inhabited from the Early Bronze Age through the early Roman period and has a notable Hellenistic phase.
Tel Be'er Sheva is an archeological site in southern Israel that is believed to be the location of the remains of the biblical town of Beersheba.

Tell Abu Dhahir is located on the right bank of the Tigris River, 90 km northwest of Mosul. The British Archaeological Expedition in Iraq conducted excavations there between October 1985 and April 1986, in advance of the completion of the Eski Mosul Dam project. The pluristratified tell documents the remains of numerous cultures, including Hassuna, Ubaid, Uruk, Ninevite V, Akkadian, Khabur, Late Assyrian, and Hellenistic/Parthian phases.
Tell Abu Marya/[Apqu] was a settlement of western Assyria, the modern Tell Abu Marya.
Tell Abu Salabikh was the site of a small Sumerian city of the third millennium BC.
Tell Arbid is an archaeological site located in Syria's Al-Hasakah Governorate in the basin of the Khabur River. The site is active from the third millennium BCE onward.
Tell Brak, located in the Upper Khabur of northeastern Syria, was occupied between the sixth and second millennia BCE. The tell stands ca. 40 m tall and covers ca. 130 hectares.

Tell Grai Darki was the site of a Hellenistic and Roman settlement. The site is located approximately 2 km north of Tell Deir Situn. John Curtis conducted excavations here as part of the Saddam Dam Salvage Project.

Tell Hammam al-Turkmen is an ancient settlement mound or tell located on the left bank of the Balikh river, approximately 80 km north of Raqqa, Syria. The tell has a diameter of 500 meters and stands 45 meters tall.

Tell Zurghul is an archaeological site in Iraq covering approximately 70 ha. The site includes two settlement mounds. The ancient site was located on a canal leading away from Lagash, some 10 km to the southeast. The ancient name of this place was Niĝin (or Nina or Ninua), and Nanshe (Nanše) was the titular divinity.

Tell al-Lahm is probably to be identified with Dur-Yakin, Duru(m), and/or Kissik, which are mentioned in Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian sources, and also in some first-millennium BCE texts together with Ur, Uruk, Larsa, Eridu, and Kullab (Uruk sanctuary).
Tell site at the northern edge of the Nablus Range inhabited from the Iron Age to the present.

Tell ‘Acharneh is located 35 km northwest of Hama, on the north bank of the Orontes River, at the crossroads of two main trade routes. This center for the production of oil, wax, and wheat was occupied during the Bronze and Iron Ages, as well as during the First Crusades. Its ancient name, Tunip, is known from second-millennium-BC sources. A stele fragment bearing an inscription of the Neo-Assyrian king Sargon II (r. 721–705 BCE) found there attests to the city’s occupation during the Iron Age.
Telmessos (modern Fethiye) was an ancient city of Lycia.
Temenion was located in the Argolid. It was built by Temenus, the son of Aristomachus. Temenion lay 50 stades from Nauplia and 26 from Argos.
Temporary Roman camp of Flavian date
Temporary Roman marching camp

Tenea was an ancient city of the Corinthia famous for its sanctuary of Apollo. Scholars have long believed it is to be located in the area of modern Chiliomodi in Greece. Recent scientific excavations have identified the general extent of a large, multi-period cemetery zone to the east and south of the modern town, as well as an extensive bath complex of Roman date.
Tenedo lies at the confluence of the Aare and the Rhine. In pre-Roman times, a key trade route crossed the River Rhine here.
Tepe Hissar, the site of an ancient settlement near Damghan in north-eastern Iran.

Tergeste (the modern Trieste) was first a vicus dependent on Aquileia (ca. 100 BC) and later became a colony under Caesar, sometime before 52 B.C. In the Augustan reorganization of Italy, the city was part of the Decima Regio and then of Venetia et Histria. By Late Antiquity, it had become a bishopric.

Termitito is located in the hinterland of the ancient city of Herakleia in Lucania (in the vicinity of present-day Policoro. Herakleia and its hinterland have been the subject of extensive fieldwork. The remains of a Roman villa have been excavated at Termitito. Giardino 1994 notes that Roman-period sites that developed in this area had various objectives in terms of landscape exploitation. The situation of this villa aims to exploit the scenographic potential of its position.
Terventum was the site of a Roman municipium established in the territory of the Pentrian Samnites.
Teurnia, on the Drau river, was an ancient settlement of Noricum.
Th(e)rambos was the southeasternmost city on the Pallene peninsula.
Thabraca was a maritime city of Numidia located at the mouth of the river Tusca.
Thaima or Tayma is an oasis with a long history of human settlement.

Thala (Tell Halif) is a small tell located in the northeastern Negev desert, near the modern town of Lahav. The site shows signs of habitation from the Chalcolithic through the Medieval and Ottoman periods.
The "VIllage of the Ilians" located on the slopes of Karatepe in Asiatic Turkey.
The Archaic to Classical period settlement of Mekyberna served as a port city for Olynthos. (Kalyves Polygyrou, Halkidiki Macedonia).
The Asklepieion at Pergamon is located 3 km south of the Acropolis.
The Bahariya Oasis is a depression and oasis located in the Western Desert of Egypt approximately 370 km from Cairo.
The Barrington Atlas Directory indicates that an ancient place called Pedum could correspond to the modern Corcolle in Lazio, Italy.

The Barrington Atlas provides two possible alternative modern identifications along the Eisack/Iscara river in South Tyrol for the location of ancient Sublavione, which is attested both on the Peutinger map and in the Antonine Itineraries: Waidbruck/Ponte Gardena and Klausen/Chiusa.

The Castellum Laurum along the frontier in Germania Inferior was built first in the AD 40s and then destroyed during the Batavian Revolt of AD 69. The rebuilt fort remained in use until the early fifth century.

The Chalcolithic settlement site of Chogha Mish, also known as Tappeh-ye Choghā Mīsh, dates originally to the early seventh millennium BCE and is located on the Susiana Plain of western Iran. The site was occupied continuously from the Neolithic period to the Proto-Literate period. It was eventually eclipsed by nearby Susa, but BAtlDir maintains its occupation through at least the end of the early Roman imperial period, and possibly later.
The Civita di Bagnoregio was originally founded by the Etruscans.
The Egyptian site of Thonis, sometimes referred to as Thonis-Heracleion, was located near the Canopic Mouth of the Nile, approximately 32 km northeast of Alexandria. Its ruins are now submerged.
The Etruscan Vatluna resisted Rome's influence in the seventh century BCE, although the city may have been the source of Rome's adoption of the curule chair and the fasces.
The Etruscan settlement of *Hurta (the modern Orte) was close to the Vadimonis Lacus where the Romans fought, and won, two engagements against Etruscan armies.

The Hellenistic-Roman city of Cantha, now Qanawat in Syria, is located in the Hauran region. While it likely has earlier phases, perhaps as the Kenath of the Hebrew Bible, it is first mentioned during the reign of Herod the Great. Septimius Severus bestowed colonial status upon the city.

The Latin town of Nomentum and Rome were linked by means of the Via Nomentana. In Livy's history the town, a member of the Latin League, is captured by Lucius Tarquinius Priscus. Nomentum was one of a number of towns captured by Tarquinius. The Romans granted the town civitas sine suffragio after 338 B.C.
The Nabataean city of Mampsis or Memphis (Ancient Greek: Μέμφις) was an important station on the Incense Road.
The Niederbieber fort was a Roman border fort of the Upper German Limes. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.
The Pagus Vescinus is only attested epigraphically.

The Peutinger map situates "Namare" in modern Austria on an ancient road between "Trigisamo" (also unlocated) and "Arelate" (Arelape, modern Pöchlarn). For decades, scholars have speculated that Namare might have been a Roman fort, situated at what is now Melk; however, despite some finds over the years, this theory has not been archaeologically proven. More recently, purported archaeological finds at nearby Großpriel have provided a possible alternative identification.
The Phoenician city of Akko was re-founded by Ptolemy II Philadelphos from ca. 285-246 B.C.
The Phoenicians established a commercial outpost at Tripolis (Tripoli) in the ninth century BC. An independent city during the Hellenistic period, Tripolis came under Roman control in 64 BC.
The Ptolemaic temple to Hathor at Dendera.
The Ptolemaic temple to Sobek and Horus the Elder at Kom Ombo.

The Roman Fort near Watercrook Farm (at Kendal in northwest England) was originally built ca. AD 90 and rebuilt ca. AD 130. It may have been called Alone?/Alauna? in antiquity. Its poorly preserved remains are coincident with those of a contemporaneous civilian settlement.
The Roman Legio VII Gemina was based in Tarraconensis and gave its name to the settlement. This ancient place is now León, Spain, which is built atop the ancient settlement.

The Roman capital of Creta et Cyrenaica province, then Creta, and later seat of the Archbishop of Crete, Gortyna was a thriving community from the Geometric period to the Middle Byzantine period. The first traces of urban settlement date from the Archaic period. The ancient Greek law code known as the "Gortyn Code" was discovered there in 1884.
The Roman capital of Dacia established by Trajan and located some 40 km from the indigenous center of Sarmizegetusa Regia (cited: BAtlas 21 E4 Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa)
The Roman fort at Banna, now known as Birdoswald Roman fort.
The Roman fort at Oberhochstatt is one of the least well-known Roman castra of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes.
The Roman fort at Rutupiae was erected at the location where the Claudian landings took place in A.D. 43.

The Roman fort at Theilenhofen, called Iciniacum in antiquity, was a Roman military camp along the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes. The site lies to the northwest of the village of Theilenhofen in the Weißenburg-Gunzenhausen district of Bavaria. The fort was probably built in the middle of the third century CE.
The Roman fort at modern day Tomen y Mur, presumably Flavian in date, was likely abandoned by the middle of the second century A.D.
The Roman fort of Maia located at Bowness-on-Solway, was part of the Roman defenses supporting Hadrian's Wall along the Cumbrian coast.

The Roman fort of Sibrium, known today as Castelseprio or Castel Seprio, became a significant Lombard town of the early Middle Ages. It was destroyed and abandoned in 1287. In 2011, the site, including the church of Santa Maria 'foris portas', the castrum and its Torba Tower, was enrolled as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The Siwa Oasis was, in antiquity, the site of the oracular temple of Amun (Zeus Ammon).
The Thriasion Lager was a fortified camp in ancient Attica located 3 km. west of the so-called Dema Wall.

The Vicus Augustanus Laurentium is an ancient settlement in coastal Latium located between the shore and the Via Severiana. The site was first described by Rodolfo Lanciani in 1903. The British School at Rome carried out excavations in the 1980s.
The Wadi es-Sebua, also known as the Valley of the Lions, is the site of two New Kingdom Egyptian temples. This includes a temple built by Pharaoh Ramesses II (19th Dynasty).

The ancient Apis may correspond to the site of Zawiyet Umm el-Rakham where a substantial Pharaonic fortress of the New Kingdom is known. Zawiyet Umm ar-Racham is located about 310 km west of Alexandria. The site was identified in 1946 and was sporadically examined until scientific excavations under Steven Snape were carried out between 1994 and 2001.
The ancient Black Sea settlement of Odessus is now Varna, Bulgaria.
The ancient Greek and Roman city of Corinth, located in the Peloponnese, Greece. Also known today as Archaia Korinthos and not to be confused with the nearby modern town.
The ancient Roman town of Alcester, United Kingdom
The ancient Roman town of Iader (Iadera), given status of a Roman colony in 48 B.C.
The ancient Saronic Gulf port of Corinth (near modern Kechries in Greece).

The ancient Thracian city of Xantheia, located somewhere in the vicinity of ancient Maroneia (modern Ag. Kharalabos in the Greek administrative region of Eastern Macedonia and Thrace). No archaeological evidence connects the ancient city with the more recent location that now bears its name. BAtlas tentatively and approximately placed (hollow symbol) ancient Xantheia some 50 kilometers east-southeast of modern Xanthi and 7 kilometers west of ancient Maroneia.
The ancient capital of Messenia; its excavated monumental remains lie immediately south and west of the modern Greek village of Mavrommati.
The ancient capital of the Thessalian Pelasgiotis, modern Larisa in Greece.
The ancient center of the Aurunci, Suessa Aurunca was abandoned in 337 B.C. for a more favorable site (modern Sessa) where a Latin colony was established in 313 B.C.

The ancient city of Aleppo, located in modern Syria, where extensive elements of Hittite, Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Ayyubid, and Umayyad architecture are incorporated into the urban fabric of the modern city. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986.
The ancient city of Babylon began as an Akkadian city-state founded by Amorites in 1894 B.C. The city was also the seat of the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 608 to 539 B.C.
The ancient city of Bostra (modern Busra in Syria), where extensive ancient Nabataean, Roman, Byzantine, and Umayyad structures still visible. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1980.
The ancient city of Carthage, located in modern Tunis (Tunisia). Carthage engaged the Roman state in a series of wars conventionally referred to as the Punic Wars by scholars.
The ancient city of Damascus, located in modern Syria, with some 125 monuments dating back to the Roman period. Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.
The ancient city of Elea / Velia was said to have been founded by Phocaean Greeks in the sixth century B.C. and then became an ally of Rome in the third century B.C.
The ancient city of Emona (now modern Ljubljana).
The ancient city of Ithaca on the homonymous Aegean island. Following RE, BAtlas locates it at the small, protected harbor of Polis on the island's northwest coast.

The ancient city of Kakyron, said to have been founded by the Sicani in the eighth century B.C., is probably to be identified with the remains of a fortified city, north of Licata, located on the western side of Sicily.

The ancient city of Nicopolis ad Istrum is located near the village of Nikyup, Bulgaria, in the district of Veliko Turnovo. The Roman emperor Trajan founded Nicopolis ad Istrum following victories over the Dacians in 101 and 106 CE. The fortified Roman city had an area of approximately 30 ha.

The ancient city of Rusuccuru was founded as a Punic settlement on the Oued Sebaou river. In the Roman period, an inscription indicates that Rusuccuru achieved the status of municipium under Septimius Severus, yet some sources continue to refer to it as a colonia.

The ancient city of Salamis was located on the Saronic island of the same name, overlooking the modern Ampelaki Bay to the east. The site was likely largely in the area now covered by the modern city of Ambelaki/Ampelaki.
The ancient city of Swenett in Egypt, called Syene by the Greeks.
The ancient city of Thebes in Boeotia (modern Greece).
The ancient city of Tyre (modern es-Sur on the coast of Lebanon). A UNESCO World Heritage Site, in part because of its "important archaeological remains, mainly from Roman times."

The ancient name of this fortified grain-house is known only from a Latin inscription describing its restoration by a governor of Mauretaniae Caesariensis in the mid 290s CE under Diocletain and his tetrarchic colleagues. The inscription's findspot, near a spring in Algeria's Kefrida Pass depression, is close to remains of Roman fortifications noticed by French scholars in the 19th century on either side of the pass. They presumably guarded a road that ran south from Muslubium, as well as water sources (the "Aqua Frigida" itself?) supplying Muslubium via a recently discovered aqueduct (Ouaret Ladjouze). The modern toponymic component "K'frida" presumably reflects the ancient "Frigida".
The ancient panhellenic sanctuary of Delphi in Greece, seat of the oracle of Apollo.
The ancient port city in Egypt's Nile Delta, founded by Alexander the Great in 332/331 BCE.
The ancient settlement of Apollonopolis Parva/Diocletianopolis, modern Qus.
The ancient settlement of Delos, located on the Aegean island of the same name.

The ancient settlement of Fratte is located near Salerno, Italy. The settlement is situated in the valley of the Irno River and was likely first settled by Etruscans in the sixth century BCE. Material remains ascribed to both Etruscan and Samnite cultures have been identified at the site.
The ancient settlement of Panapio/Punicum corresponds to present-day Santa Marinella, Rome, Italy.

The ancient settlement of Pontecagnano is located on the plain of the Sele river, about 4 km from the sea. Settlement begins in the Chalcolithic period. The Early Iron Age sees the arrival of people identified as Villanovans who originated in South Etruria, initiating a proto-urban phase of the settlement covering some 80 ha.
The ancient settlement of Shams el-Din in Egypt's Kharga Oasis, which contains a necropolis and a 4th-century CE church.
The ancient settlement of Talabriga is probably to be associated with the Portuguese archaeological site known today as Cabeço do Vouga.
The ancient site of Legio was a Roman military camp located south of Tel Megiddo in the Roman province of Galilee. Legio VI Ferrata was stationed there following the Bar Kokhba revolt.
The ancient village of Tineida, in Egypt's Dakhleh Oasis.
The ancient, fortified port settlement of ancient Athens. It was also the coastal deme of the tribe Hippothoontis.

The archaeological remains of an Etruscan settlement were discovered at San Giovenale, close to Blera, Italy, by the Swedish Institute at Rome in the 1950s and 1960s. The ancient name of the site is unknown.

The archaeological site of Kommos was a Bronze Age port and settlement in southern Crete with subsequent habitation and monumental construction dating to the Hellenistic and Roman periods. This site is possibly to be identified with Amyklaion, mentioned in contemporary sources.
The archaeological site of Marina el-Alamein.

The archaeological site of Timpone del Ponto in Lucania indicates occupation from the Bronze Age through to the the Hellenistic period. The built fortifications of the Hellenistic period command a narrow point of the Sinni river valley between the hills of Coppola and Colobraro.

The attested Hellenistic settlement of "Taulara" may be identified with a now-invisible castle site at modern Horoztepe in Turkey's Tokat province (BAtlas, following Olshausen who argues for a location in the area between Tokat and Horoztepe, but does not commit to the latter).
The capital city of Seleucus I Nicator, established ca. 300 BCE.
The capital city of ancient Phrygia, the ruins of Gordion are located near the modern village of Yassıhüyük about 10km east of the Turkish city of Polatlı.

The capital city of the Hermopolite nome (the fifteenth Nome of Upper Egypt). The ancient Egyptians called the site Khmun after the group of eight divinities (Ogdoad) that represented the primordial world.
The capital city of the ancient Berber Kingdom of Numidia.
The capital city of the ancient Bruttii in Calabria.
The capital city of the first dynasties of ancient Egypt. While the precise location of the ancient site is unclear, mainstream scholarly thought places it near ancient Abydos and modern Girga.
The capital of Astyages (Istuvegü), captured by Cyrus the Great in 549 BCE. The site served as a summer residence for both Persian and Parthian kings.
The capital of the Remi in Gallia Belgica, now Reims.
The capital of the Roman Republic and Empire.
The capital of the seventh Nome of Upper Egypt, located on the west bank of the Nile.
The chief ancient city (civitas) of the Treveri. Modern Trier in Germany.
The chief base of the Roman fleet on the lower Danube river.
The chief settlement of the Nantuates.
The chief town of the Dalmatae.
The chief town of the Vaccaei in the northern part of Hispania Tarraconensis.
The chief, homonymous city on the Cycladic island of Kythnos (modern Vriokastro/Episkopi).

The city of Apollonopolis Magna was located on the west bank of the Nile, south of Thebes. As the seat of Horus, Greeks regarded it as a site connected with Apollo. It served as the capital of the second nome of Upper Egypt.
The city of Aqaba on the Red Sea.
The city of Jerusalem.
The city of Nola (Nuvlana) is considered one of the oldest in Campania. Under Augustus, the settlement became a Roman colony; it was the spot where Augustus died in A.D. 14.
The city of Venice in northern Italy.
The colonial city of Katane (modern Catania) was founded by Chalcidian Greeks sometime after the foundation of Leontini in 730 B.C.

The compilers of the Barrington Atlas include two ancient places called "Duronia" on map 44. This instance of Duronia corresponds to a fortified Samnite settlement that S.P. Oakley refers to as "Civita di Duronia". This place corresponds to a present-day Italian comune located in the province of Campobasso. As is often true with the observable settlement pattern, the ancient fortified center occupies an elevated position while its post-ancient successor (in this case, the source of the toponym) eschews the high ground for more level terrain. The difference in elevation between the ancient fortified center and the present-day Duronia is more than 120 meters.

The complex at Qasr el-Hallabat began as a Roman frontier fort along the Via Nova Traiana under the emperor Caracalla. There is evidence for pre-Roman activity at the site (Nabatean). By the eighth century, the Umayyad caliph Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik ordered that the Roman structures be demolished in order to redevelop the outpost as an Umayyad desert complex.
The earliest Roman fort in present-day Gelligaer, Wales.
The early settlement history of [Feraria] (modern Ferrara) remains uncertain. The name Ferrara appears in AD 753 in a document of the Lombard king Desiderius.
The earthwork remains of a Roman fort that likely covered an area of approximately 2 ha.
The eleventh century monastery of Santa Maria di Monteverde sits atop and reuses elements of Roman and pre-Roman settlements on the hilltop.
The encampment of the Cohors I Celtiberorum equitata civium Romanorum, an auxiliary unit of the Roman army.

The environs of Corciano were inhabited by Etruscans and, later, there is evidence for Roman villas. In 1812, a series of bronze panels from an Etruscan parade chariot was discovered at Castel San Mariano di Corciano.
The eponymous settlement of the island of Corcyra (modern Korfu).
The eponymous settlement of the volcanic island of Nisyros in the Aegean Sea.
The fortified port settlement at Sounion, a coastal deme of Leontis, served the Athenian grain ships originating in Euboea and was the site of the sanctuary of Poseidon, among others.

The fourth century B.C. capital of the Ingauni Ligures sided with Carthage during the Punic War but was reduced by Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus in 181 B.C. A treaty was struck with Rome; the city received Roman citizenship in 45 B.C.
The fourth fort on Hadrian's Wall, after Segedunum (Wallsend), Pons Aelius (Newcastle), and Condercum (Benwell).
The great ancient maritime port of Rome, located on the right-hand bank of the Tiber River.

The hamlet of Malborghetto, located on the ancient Via Flaminia, is traditionally linked with Constantine the Great and his visions of victory that occurred prior to the battle of Saxa Rubra on 28 October A.D. 312. The quadrifons arch, dating to the fourth century, marks the intersection of the Via Flaminia and the Via Tiberina.
The homonymous ancient settlement on the Dodecanese island of Kasos, which was located at modern Kastro/Poli.
The homonymous polis and settlement on the Aegean island of Paros.
The homonymous settlement on the Aegean island, located on its north shore (modern Paleopolis).

The initial, mainland site of the city, located to the southwest of modern Urla Iskelesi in Turkey. Pausanias reports that the city relocated to an island in the Bay of Smyrna, for which see "Klazomenai (later)."

The legendary birthplace of the goddess Aphrodite, (Nea) Paphos has been a center of activity since the Final Bronze Age when Mycenaeans honored the goddess there. The site was listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1980.
The main city and port of the Kimmerian Bosporus, founded by Miletus in the late seventh or early sixth centuries B.C. Modern Kerch.
The modern Algerian settlement of Morsott is possibly to be identified with ancient Vasampus, attested in the Peutinger map.
The modern Farasan Islands.

The modern Greek village of Dimini in Thessaly lends its name to important prehistoric and Bronze Age settlements whose remains lie in its vicinity. In the 20th century, some scholars attempted to assign the placename "Aison" (reported by Stephanus of Byzantium) here as well, but others now reject the name entirely as false. The vicinity was abandoned at the end of the thirteenth century BCE and not reoccupied until modern times.

The modern Turkish name Kadıkalesi denotes a modern coastal neighborhood in Turkey's Aydın province, the extensive Byzantine fortified settlement (sometimes "Kadı Kalesi") that gave the neighborhood its name, and the multi-period mound on which the remains of the Byzantine castle stand wherein there is evidence for human settlement extending back to the Calcolithic. The mound and vicinity were clearly important in Hittite, Greek, Roman, and Byzantine periods.

The modern city of Faqous in the southeastern portion of the Nile delta is thought to have been built atop an ancient city known to the Greeks as Phakoussa. Strabo identifies it as the terminus of an ancient canal connecting to the Red Sea.

The modern town of Aidepsos (formerly Lispo) in Greece, is usually identified as the original city and/or polis center of ancient Aidepsos. This location lies some three kilometers north of the extensive archaeologically attested spa center at modern Loutra Aidepsou.
The modern town of Fournoi on the largest of the Aegean islands of the same name was likely the principal settlement and harbor of the archipelago, inheriting from them the name Korsiai.
The modern village of al-Karmil in the West Bank is the site of Biblical "Carmel". The site remained active in the Roman, Byzantine, and Ayyubid/Crusader periods.
The modern-day site of a Roman-British settlement dates from the second to fourth centuries AD.
The modern-day site of a Romano-British settlement dating from first and second centuries A.D.

The name of the ancient city of Arrapha is first attested in the time of the Neo-Sumerian empire. It later became part of the Akkadian empire. Its location is thought to be that of modern Kirkuk in northeastern Iraq.
The one-time capital of the ancient Kerma culture in Nubia.

The original Roman settlement at Mogontiacum (modern Mainz) was established by Drusus ca. 13/12 BC. The settlement became an important military center throughout Roman times and was the base of operations for numerous Roman legions.

The original location of the ancient city of Pleuron, which was reportedly destroyed in the third century BCE. There is debate concerning its location. After the destruction, a new site was selected for the city. It is known as "Nea Pleuron" (q.v.).
The origins of (H)Enna are unclear. Some sources claim it was founded by Syracuse in 664 B.C., but the archaeological record suggests it is likely a Hellenized Sikel settlement.
The port city of Roman Pisa.
The port city of ancient Rome located at the mouth of the river Tiber.
The port of ancient Corinth.
The port of the Etruscan city of Tarquinia.
The prehistoric settlement at Choirokoitia, in Cyprus. The site was inhabited from the seventh to the fourth millennium B.C. and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998.
The presumptive archaeological site of the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest (A.D. 9).
The primary ancient settlement and port on the island of Samos (modern Sami).
The primary ancient settlement on the Aegean island of the same name.
The primary center of the Redones tribe. Modern Rennes in France.
The primary city of the Veneti in Gallia Lugdunensis (modern Vannes).
The principal ancient city on the Aegean island of Chios.
The remains of a Roman fort and its annex located on the left bank of the River Isla. The site was first identified by Eric Bradley in 1941 and again re-confirmed in 1977.
The remains of a Roman fort and settlement located at Catterick, North Yorkshire.
The remains of a first-century A.D. earthwork and the buried remains of a Roman fort at Slack. These remains might be associated with the Roman toponym Camulodonum.

The ritual and political capital of Upper Egypt at the end of the Predynastic period and the Early Dynastic Period, with occupation beginning as early as Naqada I. The site was an important ritual center for the worship of Horus.

The site of Ilici began as a pre-Roman settlement that eventually developed into a Roman municipium. The site continued into the Visigothic and Byzantine periods as a minor urban settlement, controlling a vast territory which reached old Lucentum. The settlement was relocated to the modern site of Elche in the Islamic period.
The site of Palma, on the island of Majorca, experienced multiple phases of settlement from Talaiotic to Roman.

The site of Teichos Dymaion is located in Achaea and was continuously occupied in antiquity. Its megalithic fortifications date to the time of the Mycenaeans. In the first millennium BCE, the site's strategic value makes it a factor in third-century warfare. The site continued to be used during the Byzantine period, was used by the Venetians, and factored in World War II when extensive military works built at the site wreaked havoc on the ancient remains.
The site of Tell Mahuz site in northern Iraq was occupied from the fourth millennium B.C. to the Early Islamic Period.

The site of Thalamai was evidently in an area known in modern times as Svina, in the eastern portion of modern Thalames/Koutiphari on the west side of the Mani peninsula at the base of the Taygetos mountains. Evidence for human habitation here stretches back to the Neolithic. In ancient times, this Laconian/Messenian settlement was home to Spartan perioikoi and, according to Pausanias, was the site of an oracle of Ino/Pasiphae.

The site of a Bronze Age terramare settlement, Parma was re-founded first by Etruscans and later by the Romans when a colony was established there in 183 B.C. The city was rebuilt by Augustus and was eventually sacked by Attila.
The site of a Middle Bronze Age village located on the Scogli di Apani archipelago near Brindisi, Italy.
The site of a Phoenician port on the Gulf of Oristano in western Sardinia.
The site of a Roman Saxon Shore fort known as "Walton Castle". The fort was built ca. A.D. 276-285 and was destroyed by sea erosion in the eighteenth century.
The site of a Roman and Iron Age settlement located at Kelvedon.
The site of a Roman fort and fortlet on the Antonine Wall.
The site of a Roman fort at Burrow in Lonsdale.
The site of a Roman fort at Newcastle dating between the second and fourth centuries. The fort was perhaps designed to protect a bridge over the river Tyne.
The site of a Roman fort in Wales occupied during the late first and early second centuries A.D.
The site of a Roman fort in the eastern desert of Egypt.
The site of a Roman fort occupied during the Antonine period near present-day Musselburgh in East Lothian.
The site of a Roman fort on the Antonine Wall.
The site of a Roman fort on the right bank of the Danube, Transdierna played an important part in the Dacian Wars. Its name is not attested until the fourth century A.D.
The site of a Roman fort on the river Waal.
The site of a Roman fortlet on the Antonine Wall. The fortlet measures ca. 21.5 x 18.5 m, covering an area of ca. 0.04 ha.
The site of a Roman legionary fortress, municipium, and colonia at modern-day York, England.
The site of a Romano-British Settlement is located at Little London, Chigwell. The site is located above the flood plain of the River Roding.
The site of a large Roman town located on the Troia peninsula on the left bank of the Sado river.
The site of an ancient port facility located at the southern tip of the Akrotiri Peninsula, Cyprus. The archaeological remains date to the fifth and sixth centuries CE.
The site of an important Isis sanctuary in Lower Egypt. Behbeit el-Hagar is located along the Damietta branch of the Nile River, north of Sebennytos and 8 kilometers west of Mansoura.

The site of this ancient settlement, which provides evidence for habitation from the Bronze Age into late antiquity, lies just to the north of the modern settlement that has inherited its name (Kabile) in the Bulgarian province of Yambol.

The small hill that is known as "Il Poggio di Serrone di Bove" is located in the hinterland of ancient Norba and was the site of ancient settlement activity. Architectural remains on the site include those of a polygonal masonry sub-struction or platform as well as an ancient roadway that may be part of the road tract from Norba to Cora.
The so-called "Arcadian Orchomenos", located near a modern village in the Peloponnese that, until the 1960s, was known as Kalpaki.

The so-called "Boeotian Orchomenos", located in the vicinity of the Byzantine church of Panaghia Skripou. The longer, modern title is used to distinguish this settlement from another Greek site with the same ancient name located in Arcadia in the Peloponnese.
The so-called "Summer Palace of Nebuchadnezzar," located at ancient Babylon in modern Iraq.
The so-called Thracian (or Macedonian) Methone is an unlocated settlement attested by ancient sources. Modern scholars suggest Moustheni as a possible identification.

The surviving manuscript of Skylax reports a Methana in the Thyreatis plain on the Gulf of Argolis. The toponym is widely thought to be a corruption of Anthana/Anthane, known from other sources. This place "may have been one of two known coastal forts in the area ... probably Nisi Agiou Andrea" (Shipley's 2019 commentary on Skylax, page 129 note 46).

The toponym Amplero refers to an archaeological area located to the northeast of Collelongo (L'Aquila) in Italy. The Institute of Archaeology at the University of Pisa conducted fieldwork at the site in 1969-1971.
The town of Forum Livii in Gallia Cispadana is located on the right bank of the Montone River.
The village of San Casciano dei Bagni, located south of Siena, Italy, has been frequented since at least the first millennium BCE on account of its thermal springs with supposedly healing properties.
The visible archaeological remains of the settlement of Aunobari cover ca. 5 hectares.

The westernmost of the "three cities" of Tripolis, Abrotonum/Sabratha was founded ca. 500 B.C. by the Phoenicians. The city was part of the Numidian Kingdom of Massinissa before becoming a Roman city.
The westernmost town of ancient Egypt.

Thelepte was a Roman city in Africa Byzacena. It achieved municipal status perhaps in the time of Vespasian and became a colonia under Trajan. The city played an important administrative role in fourth century AD north Africa.

Theopompus mentions Chalia as a town of Boeotia. It is also attested epigraphically and may have been a member of the Boeotian league. Fossey locates the city in the vicinity of the church of Agios Minas in modern Drosia. Archaeological finds in the area indicate human activity from as early as the Bronze Age.

There is evidence for human habitation from the Neolithic onward In and around Paradeisos, a modern Greek village in the Nestos municipality of Kavala, Macedonia and Thrace. Long-standing scholarly consensus holds that these remains are to be identified with the well-attested ancient settlement of Topeiros, although BAtlDir registers slight hesitation (question mark).

There was likely a Thracian settlement in the vicinity of modern Shoumen/Shumen in Bulgaria prior to Roman and subsequent occupation. Remains of a late antique complex of structures with associated churches has been identified beneath the remains of a multi-phase fortress on high ground to the west of the modern city.
Thermopylae is the name of a narrow pass leading from Thessaly into Locris. It was the site of a pivotal battle during the Graeco-Persian wars in 480 BC.
Thespiai was an ancient city of Boeotia, located at the foot of Mt. Helicon.
Theveste (modern Tébessa, Algeria) became a Roman center and, in the Imperial period, the Legio III Augusta was raised there. In later times Theveste is connected with the Donatists.
This Roman theater in the modern French commune of Thénac was discovered in the 19th century. Its presence implies an ancient settlement or extra-urban sanctuary.

This ancient city, located near modern Volos in Thessaly, was founded by Demetrios Poliorketes in the third century BCE and abandoned in the 6th century CE. Continuous human activity in the area can be traced back at least as early as the Neolithic.
This ancient settlement is thought to have been located at modern Monte de S. Maria/Redondo (Fiães parish, Feira municipality) in Portugal.

This ancient settlement located on the Gulf of Mirabello at modern Pakheia Ammos in Lasithi, east Crete, has produced archaeological remains dating from Minoan times through the Greek and Roman periods.

This ancient settlement site, with remains of a fortified acropolis and lower town, is located just south of modern Ag. Marina in Thessaly (Greece). Modern scholars consider it a likely identification for ancient Patronis/Tronis/Troneia, which is mentioned in ancient sources.

This ancient settlement, mentioned in several Roman-era itineraries and sources, has been identified with the ruin/archaeological site known in modern times as Marsa al Dajaj, which is located adjacent to the modern Algerian coastal village of Zemmouri El Bahri.

This hill, in the modern Sicilian province of Caltanissetta, was the site of a human settlement from the early Iron Age through the medieval period. It became fortified possibly as early as the late archaic period. The Castello di Mussomeli (Castello Manfredonico) was erected on the site in the 14th century CE.

This important Mesopotamian city flanks the eastern edge of the Tigris flood plain, opposite modern Mosul, of which it is now a suburb. From the third millennium B.C. onwards, Nineveh was the most important religious center of the goddess Ištar in the area that would become the Assyrian heartland. Starting in the Middle Assyrian period, the city came under the authority of the kings of Assyria, who often sponsored large-scale building activities there. However, it was not until 704 B.C. that Nineveh became the administrative capital of Assyria when the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib moved the royal family and court there and transformed the city into a thriving imperial metropolis. Nineveh remained Assyria’s capital until 612 B.C., when it was captured and destroyed by a Babylonian-Median coalition led by Nabopolassar and Cyaxares. The visible remains of the (7th-century) Assyrian city include the citadel mound Kuyunjik, the smaller mound of Nebi Yunus, and the twelve-kilometer-long city wall.
This modern site in Belgium was once home to a settlement of the Treveri (it was dubbed "Vertunum" in earlier modern literature).
This place was originally included in the Barrington Atlas as an unnamed feature. The map-by-map directory indicates that it be identified as "settlement and fort north of Bled Fachar".
This place was published as an unintended duplicate of https://pleiades.stoa.org/places/814675/.
This settlement of the Treveri (modern Neumagen in Germany) served for a time as market and road station and was later the site of a late Roman fortification. Extensive funerary remains also survive.

This vicus is mentioned on Roman inscriptions discovered in the area of modern Lecce dei Marsi in Italy. The precise location of the town is not known, but it is probably not to be found at the medieval foundation known now as "Lecce Vecchio", which was abandoned after an earthquake in the early 20th century.
Thisbe was an ancient town of Boeotia located on the southern flank of Mt. Helicon.
Thizica was a civitas in the Roman province of Africa Proconsularis.
Thorikos was a coastal deme of the tribe Akamantis, in southeastern Attica. A significant Mycenaean prescence existed at the site during the Bronze Age.

Thouria is a settlement of the Peloponnese, with archaeological evidence ranging in date from the Bronze Age to the Roman period. The nature of the archaic and classical polity is debated in the sources. The ancient site is located in the vicinity of modern Aithaia/Hellenika, about 3 kilometers north of modern Thouria.
Thubursicum Numidarum (now Khamissa, Algeria) is an indigenous site that became a Roman municipium by A.D. 100 (Municipium Ulpium Traianum Augustum Thubursicu).

Thugga/Tokai? (Dougga) is an ancient site in Tunisia with a rich heritage that includes Numidian-Berber, Punic, ancient Roman, and Byzantine phases. The city's Roman phase is particularly well preserved and UNESCO listed the site as a World Heritage Site in 1997.
Thymaitadai was a city deme of the tribe Hippothoontis in Attica, located in modern Keratsini, a western suburb of Piraeus.

Thysdrus (modern El Djem, Tunisia) was a Punic and Roman city of North Africa. It flourished in the second century A.D. and built its massive amphitheater in the third century. After an abortive revolt in A.D. 238, the city was destroyed by soldiers loyal to Maximinus Thrax.
Tiberias was founded by Herod Antipas ca. 20 BC.
Tibiscum was an ancient settlement of Dacia mentioned by Ptolemy that later became a Roman castrum and municipium.
Tigava Castra was a fort located in Mauretania Caesariensis, between Oppidum Novum and Malliana.
Tilurium was the site of the fortress of Legio VII Claudia Pia Fidelis.

Tingi (modern Tangier) began as a Carthaginian colony of the early fifth century BCE. A commercial center, Tingi came under the Roman sphere in the first century BCE, initially as a free city but later as the site of a colony (Colonia Julia) under Claudius and the capital of Mauritania Tingitana.
Tiora Matiene was the site of an ancient oracle of the god Mars. The Barrington Atlas tentatively placed it at modern Teora, near Barete.
Tipasa was an ancient Punic trading-post conquered by Rome and turned into a strategic base for the conquest of the kingdoms of Mauritania.
Tolentinum was a town of Picenum that is listed as having municipal status in the Liber Coloniarum.

Tolmo de Minateda was an early Roman hilltop oppidum located in the municipal territory of modern Helin in the Spanish autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha. It was abandoned in the second century CE and then reoccupied in Late Antiquity (ca. 590 CE) as a Visigothic episcopal see during the Byzantine-Visigothic war. It was finally abandoned in the ninth century, and the population was resettled in Murcia, a new foundation. Tolmo de Minateda has been tentatively identified with the attested placename Ilounon.
Tolosa (modern Toulouse) was a city of Gallia Narbonensis and the metropolis of the Volcae Tectosages.
Tomis was founded as a Greek colony on the Black Sea coast ca. 600 B.C.
Torikos/Pagras Limen/Heptalou Limen (modern Gelendzhik) was a Greek trading outpost on the Black Sea known to the Romans as Pagrae.
Touphion is located on the east bank of the Nile River about 20 km south of Thebes. The ruins of a multi-period temple initially built by Sesostris I were found there.
Traianoupolis in Thrace was re-founded on the site of Doriscus, a site that Darius the Great founded in 512 B.C.
Traiectum (modern Utrecht) was a fortified site along the Roman frontier (limes) of Germania Inferior. It may have been a crossing point on the Rhine river.
Tralles/Dia/Seleuceia ad Maeandrum/Kaisareia was an ancient city founded by Argives and Trallians that then fell under the sway of the Persian Empire and, later, Hellenistic kings.
Treba (modern Trevi nel Lazio) was originally a settlement of the Aequi.
Trebiae was an ancient city of Umbria (regio IV) located near the line of the Via Flaminia. It is identified with modern Trevi, north of Spoleto in Italy.
Trebula Mutuesca or Trebula Mutusca was one of two Sabine cities bearing the name Trebula.

Trevignano Romano, located on the shores of Lake Bracciano, lies some 47 km from Rome. Archaeological evidence for Etruscan occupation, in the form of tombs dating to the eighth - sixth centuries B.C., has been discovered to the north of the modern town. A medieval castle was built there under Innocent III ca. 1200.
Trikorynthos was an ancient deme of Attica.
Troesmis was an ancient town of Scythia Minor and was connected, at various times, with Legio V Macedonica and Legio II Herculia.

Tuder, modern Todi, is an ancient city of Umbria. Its foundation likely occurred during the eighth/seventh centuries BC, although legendary traditions associate the site with the activities of Herakles.
Tuficum was an ancient city of Umbria located on the Aesis River. It became a municipium of the tribus Oufentina.
Tullum was the capital of the civitas Leucorum.
Tunes was a Libyan city in Africa Proconsularis. Rome prevailed in a land battle south of Tunes in 256 BC during the First Punic War.
Tunisian location of ruins of an "agglomération urbain" tentatively identified in AAT with the attested "Elephantaria" (whence BAtlas).
Tureng tepe/Khosro-shad-Peroz is an archaeological site located in northeastern Iran.
Tusculum was a Latin city of the Alban Hills in central Italy. After 381 B.C., Tusculum became the first "municipium cum suffragio".
Tzon/Tzur (modern Derbent, Russia) was also known in antiquity as Darband, an ancient city in Dāḡestān on the western shore of the Caspian Sea.
U(r)gia was located 27 Roman miles northwest of Hasta Regia.
Uchi Maius was a township of Africa Proconsularis where Marius settled veterans. It did not achieve the status of colonia until the third century.
Ugernum was a waypoint on the Via Domitia located on the right bank of the Rhodanus fl.
Unlabeled feature captured from the Barrington Atlas

Uruk was an ancient Sumerian (and later Babylonian) city located on the Euphrates river. At its height (ca. 2900 BC), Uruk's population may have topped 50,000 people and its walls enclosed an area of more than six square kilometers, making it the largest city in the world at that point in time.
Urvinum Mataurense (modern Urbino).
Uthina was a town in the province of Africa Proconsularis with Roman colonial status.
Uxama Argaela was a Celtiberian settlement of the Arevaci. The site was subsequently conquered by the Romans.
Uzentum/Ouxenton (Ugento) was an ancient city in the territory of the Salentini with both Messapic and Roman phases.
Uzita was a settlement of Byzacium located south of Hadrumetum.
Vada Volaterrana was an Etruscan port city located north of the mouth of the Cecina River.
Vaga (Béja, Tunisia) was a much-contested city in antiquity. During the conflict against Rome, Iugurtha made Vaga his base of operations.

Vagniacis was a small Roman site of the first to fifth centuries with likely specialized religious functions. A series of five temples are situated within a temenos along the Watling Street at Springhead.
Vani (7th -1st centuries BCE) is an ancient city located in the Colchis Lowlands on the western bank of the Sulori River.
Vappincum was a pre-Roman settlement captured by the Romans in 14 BC.
Varia (modern Vicovaro) was a settlement of the Sabines.
Vasio (modern Vaison-la-Romaine) was the civitas capital of the Vocontii and eventually received Roman status by the late first century BC.

Veh Shapur/Bishapur was an ancient city in Iran on the ancient road between Persis and Elam. This ancient and medieval town in Fārs was, in the Sasanian period, the administrative center of one of the five districts in the province of Fārs.
Veleia was an ancient Ligurian settlement (regio VIII).

Velitrae (modern Velletri) was an ancient Volscian settlement. In the Roman Republican period, Velitrae was attacked by Marcus Furius Camillus (379 B.C.) and again by Cincinnatus (377 B.C.); the Romans controlled the site by 365 B.C. The gens Octavia hailed from the city and a youthful Octavian spent time there.
Venafrum was an ancient town of Campania.
Venonis was a Roman site located at the intersection of Watling Street and Fosse Way in Britannia.
Venta or Venta Icenorum was a central place, and perhaps market-town, of the Iceni, the tribe that revolted against Roman rule in 61 CE.
Venta was a Roman town in what is now Wales. Established ca. A.D. 75, Venta served as an administrative and mercantile center for the defeated Silures tribe.

Verlucio is the site of a Roman settlement. An incomplete fortified enclosure has been identified from fieldwork and aerial photographs. The site was located along the Roman road from Cunetio to Bath (Aquae Sulis).
Verona was an ancient settlement that became a Roman colonia in 89 BC and a municipium in 49 BC.
Verulae is an ancient city that became a Roman municipium in 90 B.C. Modern Veroli in Italy.
Vescellium was a settlement of the Hirpini.
Vesontion (modern Besançon) is first mentioned by Caesar in his commentaries ca. 58 BC. It is situated on a tributary of the Saône river.
Vesunna (Périgueux) was an oppidum of the Petrucorii that became part of Roman Aquitania.

Vettona (modern Bettona) is an ancient settlement of Umbria located between Perusia and Mevania. Pliny the Elder lists it among the municipalities of Umbria, and it also numbered as one of the “xv Populi Umbriae".
Vetus Salina was the site of a Roman castrum on the frontier of Pannonia Inferior.
Vibinum/Vibarna was an ancient settlement in Campania that opposed Rome during the Samnite Wars.
Vicetia (modern Vicenza) as a settlement of the Veneti in northern Italy.
Vicus Matrini was a mansio along the Via Cassia, located between Sutri and Forum Cassi. The site's name is attested on the Peutinger Table.
Vicus Spacorum (modern Vigo) was an ancient settlement located on the Atlantic coast of Galicia.
Vicus on the Meuse river along the road from Noviomagus to Atua(tu)ca.
Vindalium? is a site in Gallia Narbonensis where Domitius Ahenobarbus defeated the Allobroges (121 BC).
Vinovia was a Roman fort, now known as Binchester Roman fort, established ca. A.D. 79 to guard the crossing of Dere Street on the River Wear.
Viroconium was a large and prosperous city of Roman Britain.
Visentium (Bisenzio) was an Etruscan settlement located on the shores of Lago di Bolsena. The site has yielded especially important evidence for Iron Age and Etruscan period burials.

Vogüé (1868 and 1877) assumed that the large, square fort and bath facilities at the extinct Jebel Seis volcano in Syria were Roman (whence Dussaud 1927 whence BAtlas); however, excavations in the 1960s demonstrated that the fortification and other structures constitute an Umayyad fortified palace and associated settlement built in the late 7th to early 8th centuries CE, incorporating some elements of a pre-existing settlement, fort and/or monastery dating to the 6th century CE. There is no evidence for activity at the site in the early Roman empire.
